Kea currently memoizes derived selectors from their input values, so replacing a reducer object can recompute a selector even when the particular nested property it uses is unchanged. Redux subscriptions are also store-wide, and there is no dependency graph or health metadata to identify affected selectors, propagate invalidation, or detect selector cycles.

# Key Files and Locations

- `src/kea/context.ts` (`openContext`, `resetContext`): establish the opt-in default and a fresh engine context for each Kea context, without disturbing plugin initialization.
- `src/types.ts` (`Logic`, `MakeLogicType`, `InternalContextOptions`): describe the option, optional health function, and its returned graph and counters accurately.
- `src/core/reducers.ts` (`reducers`, `rootSelector`): reducer selectors are created here; integrate their state access with tracking rather than treating every reducer object as one indivisible dependency.
- `src/core/selectors.ts` (`selectors`, `addSelectorAndValue`): selector placeholders, input resolution, Reselect construction, default-argument wrappers, and value getters all meet here. This is the central place to preserve identity and capture selector-to-selector edges.
- `src/kea/atomic.ts` (new in the reference): houses the tracking, metadata, dependency graph, change detection, scheduling, subscriptions, and health reporting responsibilities.
- `src/core/index.ts` (`beforeReduxStore` middleware): observes the state before and after a dispatch and is a possible signal-update integration point; existing listeners and their ordering must continue to work.
- `src/kea/kea.ts` (`proxyFields`): logic wrappers proxy selected fields to built logic, so consider how the optional health API is exposed on both forms.
- `src/react/hooks.ts` (`useSelector`, `useValues`): connects selectors to React's external-store subscription; preserve the normal store subscription for non-atomic selectors and disabled mode.

# Solution Approach

Model each selector using an identity stable across placeholders and wrappers, scoped to its logic instance/path and local name. Keep leaf-to-selector edges separately from selector-to-selector edges: the former identify direct invalidations, while the latter support propagation, dependents, topological ordering, and cycle checks. Public health data should translate internal identities to paths relative to the relevant logic and local selector names.

Track actual reads while a selector computes, including reads through values supplied by input selectors, and associate each evaluation with the correct selector even when evaluations nest. Compare old and new state at the tracked granularity, collect all affected selectors for an action, then process or invalidate them in dependency order with deduplication. Preserve memoization based on actual inputs so unchanged intermediate results do not force downstream computation. Connect notifications to React without changing the disabled-mode behavior or lifecycle event ordering.

The reference demonstrates one proxy-and-scheduler direction, not proof that every detail satisfies the issue. In particular, validate its choices against the requested semantics rather than copying it mechanically.

# Implementation Directions

1. Trace context creation and selector registration first. Follow the two-pass construction in `selectors.ts`: inputs may capture an early placeholder that is subsequently replaced. Decide how every captured function maps to the same stable selector identity, including keyed logics, connected selectors, and rebuilds.
2. Add the option and public types, defaulting to false; expose health only when enabled. Initialize and clean up engine state with the context, and ensure wrapper field access does not accidentally expose a defined API in disabled mode.
3. Instrument state reads and selector computation. Separate navigating through an object from consuming a parent object so that `user.name` is recorded as a leaf, not also `user`; still handle a selector that actually returns or consumes the entire object. Maintain a stack or equivalent for nested evaluations, restore tracking on exceptions, and replace obsolete dynamic dependencies on each successful evaluation.
4. Create graph edges once input selectors can be identified, including forward references. Detect self-cycles and longer cycles during build/mount, before recursive evaluation, and throw an error containing `[KEA] Circular dependency detected`. Produce per-logic health snapshots with local dependencies, dependents, evaluation counts of the actual compute function, last invalidation cause, and a valid topological order.
5. Compare state changes to tracked reads and batch invalidations per dispatch. Test diamond and multi-level graphs, unchanged derived values, multiple changed leaves in one action, and nested dispatches; decide notification timing in relation to Redux subscribers and Kea listeners deliberately.
6. Integrate selector-specific React subscriptions where safe, retaining the standard path for ordinary selectors. Verify snapshots and subscriptions agree on the same state version and unsubscribe on unmount. Run existing lifecycle and React tests as well as focused tests in both modes.

# Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- Collection methods require their native receiver: distinguish `Map.get` from `Map.has`, track key presence even when a value is `undefined`, and track Set membership independently. Array `includes` and similar methods can read several indices and length; short-circuiting, holes, additions, removals, and nested elements deserve tests. Iteration or whole-collection reads may need broader dependencies. The requested key strings must be consistent between tracking and change detection, including keys that stringify ambiguously.
- A parent replacement, deletion, type change, or array length change must invalidate relevant descendants as well as whole-object readers. Avoid assuming object identity changes imply every leaf changed; conversely, immutable state updates are needed for identity-based shortcuts.

{"file_path": "/tmp/hint_output.md", "content": "# Feature schema persistence: implementation guide

## Problem Essence

`Igel._process_data` currently converts whatever columns arrive into arrays, after preprocessing and (for supervised models) removing targets; it neither applies `dataset.features` nor saves the training-time raw column names and order. Consequently later inputs can have a different order or width, while errors are often logged and swallowed, and ONNX export assumes four inputs regardless of the trained model.

## Key Files and Locations

- `igel/constants.py`: artifact filenames and results-directory constants; add a consistent name for the schema artifact.
- `igel/configs.py`: default artifact paths and both the default and available dataset property dictionaries. Represent the four feature options here without changing behavior when they are omitted.
- `igel/preprocessing.py`: raw DataFrame reading and preprocessing helpers. This is the natural place to fit and apply a reusable raw-feature schema, including option validation, constant and duplicate detection, and alias alignment.
- `igel/igel.py`: constructor, `_process_data`, fit, evaluation, prediction, persistence, and export. Connect schema fitting before preprocessing to artifact creation and description metadata, and connect schema loading to every later input path.
- `igel/servers/fastapi_server.py`: `/predict` converts request data into a CSV and invokes `Igel`; translate schema validation failures into an HTTP 400 with a JSON `detail` and clean up the temporary file.

## Solution Approach

Treat the raw schema as a fitted artifact, separate from the model and from the transformed model matrix. During fit, establish the ordered candidates from non-target raw columns and the include/exclude options, then drop constants and canonicalize duplicates in order. Persist the surviving canonical names, dropped-feature categories, and canonical-to-alias mapping alongside the model; copy the requested public metadata and schema path into `description.json`.

At evaluation and prediction, load that artifact instead of discovering features anew. For each canonical feature, find its canonical column or recorded aliases, verify that all supplied sources agree row by row, and construct a frame in training order under canonical names. Ignore other raw columns, then pass the aligned frame through the existing preprocessing and model path. Supervised evaluation must preserve targets separately; clustering has no target columns. Export should use the description's actual model-input width, accounting for transformations that can change width.

## Implementation Directions

1. Trace configuration loading in `Igel.__init__` and artifact paths in `configs.py`. Add defaults and a schema filename/path, and ensure fit and later commands resolve the same artifact, including when a description path or schema path is supplied explicitly.
2. In `preprocessing.py`, design a fit-time helper that validates include/exclude types, names, uniqueness, existence, and target overlap before selecting columns. Preserve include order; remove excluded candidates, then constants, then duplicates. Keep the first surviving duplicate as canonical and retain every later alias. Record `dropped_features` with `excluded`, `constant`, and `duplicate` lists even when empty, and reject an empty result.
3. Add an application helper that uses the persisted canonical order and alias groups. Collect missing canonical names for a useful error; compare all available sources in each group, including alias-only inputs, and name conflicting sources in errors. Construct output with canonical names and ignore unrelated columns.
4. Update `_process_data` immediately after reading raw data: retain supervised targets separately when needed, fit the schema only for training, and load/apply it for evaluation and prediction before encoding, imputation, scaling, or model invocation. Review each caller rather than equating the existing `fit_cluster` label with all clustering operations: clustering evaluation currently calls `_prepare_clustering_data`, so it must not accidentally refit the schema.
5. After successful training, save the schema with the model and add `feature_schema_path`, `input_features`, `dropped_features`, and `duplicate_feature_aliases` to the fit description. Consider how older descriptions or missing artifacts should behave; a fallback must not silently discard alias validation when alias metadata is available.
6. Follow error handling through `_process_data`, `evaluate`, and `_get_predictions`: their broad exception handlers currently log without re-raising. Validation errors must reach callers, and the API must catch them, remove temporary request data, and return an appropriate HTTP error rather than an apparent success or server error. Check that evaluation honors the configured model path as well.
7. Replace export's hard-coded width with metadata from the training description. Prefer the transformed width when available, otherwise use reliable recorded training shape or raw input width as appropriate; inspect one-hot encoding carefully because raw and model widths can differ.

## Problem Essence

`Igel._process_data` currently converts the columns it receives into arrays, after preprocessing and—for supervised models—removing targets. - **`igel/constants.py`** — Artifact filenames and results-directory constants. Add a consistent name for the schema artifact.

- **`backend/providers/types.ts`** — `AgentProvider`, `ProviderChatRequest`, `ProviderContext`, and `ProviderResponse` define the common boundary. The reference adds an optional tool-capability check, a tool schema, request tools, and a tool-use ID while retaining string-based context.
- **`backend/providers/anthropic.ts`** — translates provider requests and streamed API events. It needs to advertise tool support, transmit tool definitions, reconstruct tool-use input from streaming events, and convert serialized context entries back into API content blocks.
- **`backend/providers/registry.ts`** — holds agent configurations and resolves an agent's provider via `getAgent` and `getProviderForAgent`. Keep a per-recursion-path stack of agent IDs, rather than a global visited set: a repeated ID on the current path is circular, while a later independent delegation to the same agent can be valid. - **Sub-agent failure:** put the failure message in one tool-result with `is_error: true`; do not expose an ordinary sub-agent failure as a stream-level error. Handle both yielded errors and thrown exceptions.

- **Completion and streaming:** suppress nested `done` events as outer completions; retain one outer completion when appropriate. Preserve agent and session attribution, including screen-capture output, and check existing frontend consumers before changing message shapes.

# Problem Essence

The current repository has no AutoToc rule or TOC generation utility, so opting in with a marker cannot generate or refresh anything. Existing heading matching and rule infrastructure provide pieces of the behavior, but they do not by themselves coordinate marker boundaries, heading filtering, anchor generation, and the settings UI.

# Key Files and Locations

- `src/rules/auto-toc.ts` (new in the reference): the default-exported content rule, its defaults, settings controls, ignored block types, and illustrative examples. Compare `src/rules/auto-correct-common-misspellings.ts` and other existing rule builders.
- `src/utils/toc.ts` (new): the reference separates marker handling, heading extraction, formatting and anchor normalization, exclusion matching, and list rendering here.
- `src/rules-runner.ts`: imports rule modules, which triggers their registration; its ordinary loop runs registered rules. The reference adds an import, not a special-order invocation.
- `src/rules/rule-builder.ts`: provides registration and option builders. The reference broadens the generic value type of `NumberOptionBuilder`; investigate its relationship to numeric option properties and the text-backed settings control before choosing a type-safe compatible change.
- `src/lang/locale/en.ts`: English rule and option labels/descriptions, plus dropdown value labels. These keys feed the typed localization and settings UI.

Related existing code worth tracing: `src/rules.ts` wraps rule application in ignore handling; `src/utils/ignore-types.ts` substitutes and restores ignored blocks; `src/utils/regex.ts` defines `allHeadersRegex`; and `__tests__` contains the project's testing conventions.

# Solution Approach

Build a registered `RuleBuilder` rule that maps its options to a focused TOC utility. The normal `Rule.apply` path masks YAML, code, and math blocks before the rule runs and restores them afterward; do not assume a direct call to the builder's `apply` has that wrapper. Keep link and inline formatting text available so heading labels and anchors can be derived correctly.

Treat marker detection, extraction, and rendering as separate responsibilities. Find the first start marker and the first following end marker, retain the surrounding document, and generate headings from outside the existing TOC. For each eligible heading, derive display text separately from its anchor, apply exclusions, render indentation and list markers, then replace or insert the region with the required spacing. Add settings metadata and localization so the registered rule is discoverable and configurable.

# Implementation Directions

1. Follow an existing content rule's decorator, `OptionsClass`, examples, and option builders. Define all requested defaults and convert text-backed numeric settings appropriately; expose the specified dropdown, boolean, text, number, and multiline controls. Trace registration through the runner import and registry rather than adding an unnecessary special-order call.
2. In the utility, locate markers case-insensitively with whitespace tolerance. A missing start must be a strict no-op. When the end is missing, insert it without discarding the original subsequent document; when present, replace only the first matching region. Construct boundary whitespace deliberately, including after the closing marker.
3. Inspect `allHeadersRegex` capture groups and global-regex state. Collect ATX headings at allowed levels from the whole document while excluding the old TOC span and ignored blocks. Preserve heading order and compute indentation relative to the configured minimum level.
4. Separate heading display, comparison, and anchor processing. Resolve wiki and Markdown links to their visible text, remove image embeds, strip formatting for anchor calculation, remove trailing heading hashes, then normalize characters and deduplicate anchors. Explicit IDs affect the base anchor when enabled; formatting removal from displayed TOC labels is independently optional.
5. Prepare case-insensitive literal and slash-delimited regex exclusions before rendering. Decide how to handle invalid regex entries without crashing the entire lint operation. Track numbered-list increments across emitted items, not separately by heading level.
6. Add focused tests using the repository's rule test patterns, including the registered `Rule.apply` path as well as any utility tests. Verify defaults, settings wiring, examples, and repeated application.

# Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- The reference is guidance, not a substitute for the issue's contract: its marker expressions use literal spaces, and its closing-marker reconstruction does not always ensure a blank line afterward. Test tabs or other whitespace, adjacent following content, and end-of-file explicitly.
- An existing TOC title may itself be a heading; exclude the entire old region before collecting headings so it does not become an entry on the next run. Test a missing end marker, multiple markers, an end marker before the start, and idempotence.
- Ignored-block masking occurs through `Rule.apply`, not merely by declaring ignore types or calling the utility directly. Check that markers inside ignored blocks do not opt in and that placeholders restore correctly after replacement.
- `allHeadersRegex` accepts an arbitrary number of hashes, so enforce the requested ATX level range in addition to configured bounds. Check closing hashes, skipped levels, no matching headings, and a title with no entries.
- Test repeated anchors, punctuation-only headings, explicit IDs, links and images, formatted labels, literal and regex exclusions, and interactions between exclusions and duplicates. Avoid accidentally treating link destinations as visible text.
- Test both list styles, each bullet marker, global incrementing, non-default indentation, and numeric settings supplied as strings. The reference changes a shared generic to `any`; consider effects on existing rules rather than weakening unrelated behavior unnecessarily.

The guide is also saved at `/tmp/hint_output.md`. This guidance stage is read-only for the repository, so no branch, source modification, or commit was made.

## Problem Analysis

The style contract and Yoga display mapping do not support grid, so grid containers may be treated as hidden. Yoga and the renderer also lack grid sizing and placement, leaving children without grid geometry and potentially producing an undersized canvas.

## Suggested Directions

- Suggest first tracing public style props through the DOM and layout pipeline, preserving existing flex and hidden behavior.
- The core lies in a separate grid resolution pass that builds on Yoga’s initial layout and supplies geometry the renderer can consume.
- Consider track sizing, explicit and automatic placement, gaps, content measurement, and terminal-cell rounding as related concerns.
- Worth checking nested grids, overflow, static output, accessibility rendering, and changes across rerenders and display modes.
- Focus tests on public rendering behavior and the requested grid subset rather than assuming full CSS Grid semantics.

## Key Location Clues

- `src/styles.ts` — Defines public styles and maps display and gap properties to Yoga.
- `src/renderer.ts` — Renders computed geometry and determines output bounds.
- `src/components/Box.tsx` — Exposes and forwards public style props.

- `src/reconciler.ts` — Applies style changes during updates.

## Problem Analysis

Training does not preserve or enforce the raw feature names and order, so later inputs can differ silently in width or ordering. Broad error handling can conceal validation failures, while export assumes a fixed input width rather than the trained model’s actual width.

## Suggested Directions

- Consider treating the training-time raw feature schema as a separate fitted artifact, with attention to selection options, constants, duplicates, and aliases.
- Align evaluation and prediction inputs to the persisted schema before preprocessing, while keeping supervised targets separate and avoiding schema refitting during clustering evaluation.
- Review artifact paths, description metadata, and legacy or missing-schema behavior, especially where alias validation could otherwise be lost.
- Trace validation errors through prediction, evaluation, and the API so callers receive useful failures and temporary resources are cleaned up.
- Check export against the actual transformed model-input width, since encoding can change it; schema alignment alone does not persist preprocessing.
- Consider focused tests for schema round trips, reordered or conflicting inputs, targets, clustering, API errors, and export width.

## Key Location Clues

- `igel/configs.py`: Holds artifact-path defaults and dataset configuration options.
- `igel/preprocessing.py`: Reads raw data and is a natural place to consider schema fitting and alignment.

# Problem Essence

The current main ruleset routes ordinary `CREATE` statements into the unsupported-DDL path, so a `CREATE TABLE` body is not represented as a structural list of columns and constraints. The normal splitter and merger are designed for general SQL, and cannot enforce DDL-specific item boundaries, inline expressions, and closing-line rules without recognizing that structure.

# Key Files and Locations

The reference patch touches these files. The two DDL files do not yet exist in this checkout.

- **`src/sqlfmt/rules/__init__.py`** — `MAIN` orders top-level recognition before the `unsupported_ddl` fallback; this is the entry point for a supported table header. The reference also introduces a context-specific post-body ruleset here.
- **`src/sqlfmt/rules/ddl.py`** *(new)* — Defines body-specific recognition of closing parentheses, table constraints, and inline constraints, extending the core lexer rules.
- **`src/sqlfmt/actions.py`** — Actions emit nodes and enter or exit nested rulesets. The reference adds transitions for the header, matching body close, and post-body semicolon.
- **`src/sqlfmt/tokens.py`** — Token categories drive opening-bracket behavior, spacing, and lowercasing. DDL categories give subsequent stages the information they currently lack.
- **`src/sqlfmt/node_manager.py`** — Creates nodes, validates bracket matching, and calculates normalized values and spacing. A header token containing the opening parenthesis must participate correctly in its bracket stack and normalization.
- **`src/sqlfmt/node.py`** — Provides predicates and bracket-depth context for individual nodes. DDL scope and constraint predicates let formatting and parsing share the same interpretation.
- **`src/sqlfmt/line.py`** — Describes line depth, rendering, and structural predicates. DDL line classification helps distinguish body items, header, and body closer during merging.
- **`src/sqlfmt/splitter.py`** — Introduces structural line breaks, including the start of body items. Splits must distinguish body-level commas from commas nested in types or expressions.
- **`src/sqlfmt/merger.py`** — Recombines split lines subject to line-length and syntactic rules. DDL-specific guards are needed so merging does not undo required breaks, while still allowing an item’s nested fragments to recombine.
- **`src/sqlfmt/ddl.py`** *(new)* — Supplies the public value objects and extracts a table model from parsed `Line`/`Node` data independently of the input layout.

For context, `Analyzer.parse_query` produces the lines, and `QueryFormatter.format` runs splitting before merging. `tests/data/preformatted/400_create_table.sql` currently illustrates the unsupported pass-through behavior.

# Solution Approach

Treat supported `CREATE TABLE ... (` as a distinct scoped construct rather than reformatting raw SQL text afterward. Give the lexer enough context to classify the header, body items, constraints, matching close, and post-body clauses; integrate the new opener with the existing bracket stack so depth reflects nested parentheses. Keep the special rules scoped to DDL so ordinary SQL and unsupported DDL retain their existing behavior.

Use that structure in both formatting passes: split at outer body boundaries and between items, then prevent merges across those boundaries. Conversely, allow the pieces belonging to a single column, constraint argument list, or post-body clause to remain together as required. Build the public DDL model by traversing parsed nodes and their nesting, not by assuming one source line equals one item.

# Implementation Directions

1. Trace `MAIN`, rule priority, `handle_nonreserved_top_level_keyword`, and nested ruleset actions. Recognize the supported header before the generic unsupported rule, including `IF NOT EXISTS`, without capturing `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` or `... LIKE ...`. Ensure the body ruleset exits only at its matching outer close and post-body lexing returns control at the statement terminator.

2. Follow node creation and bracket validation in `NodeManager`, and the token classification properties in `TokenType`. Make the header opener increase depth and match `)`, normalize keywords and type names, and preserve quoted identifiers. Check existing prefix calculation for names followed by `(`, commas, constraint keywords, and `CHECK`; table-constraint keywords need different spacing from function and type names.

3. Inspect `LineSplitter.maybe_split_before` and `maybe_split_after`, then `LineMerger.create_merged_line` and its caller. Identify separators by body-relative depth, retain each separator exactly once, and isolate the header, body closer, individual items, post-body clauses, and semicolon. Preserve merging within nested type and argument lists, and account for comments and the existing length check instead of bypassing it globally.

4. Define the three public classes with equality based on their specified public fields. Use independent default lists for table constraints; compute the count and filtered-column properties from the current lists. Implement the column string marker only when the flag is true.

5. In `parse_ddl_table`, traverse nodes in source order, locate a supported table opener, and partition its body at commas at the outer body depth. Classify each item by its first meaningful token, including bare `CHECK` and named `CONSTRAINT`; do not treat nested commas or inline constraint arguments as new columns. Reconstruct each type from its original token prefixes and normalized values, ending at the first applicable inline constraint at the column’s outer depth. Return `None` for a non-table query.

6. Add focused tests alongside existing unit and functional tests. Exercise parsing directly through the analyzer as well as formatting, and compare output and parsed public values; check idempotence and existing non-DDL regressions.

# Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- The reference patch is a design guide, not a substitute for checking every stated requirement. Verify narrow line lengths, long indivisible items, semicolon placement, and all forms of post-body clauses explicitly. Only minimally overlong column definitions and post-body clause lines receive the stated length exception; table constraints are not included in that exception.
- Input can be flat, already multiline, or broken at arbitrary token boundaries. Do not use formatted line boundaries to determine columns. Preserve original inter-token whitespace in `type_name`, rather than joining values with invented spaces; distinguish original `token.prefix` from formatted `Node.prefix`.
- Nested type parameters, function calls, `REFERENCES` targets, and constraint expressions can contain commas or nested parentheses. `CHECK (` and table-constraint argument lists require a space, whereas a name immediately followed by `(` does not. Test both inline and table-level uses.
- Match constraint keywords at the appropriate depth: a keyword within a nested expression should not prematurely terminate a type or start another table item. Test constrained and unconstrained columns, named constraints, bare checks, and empty/default lists.
- Quoted and qualified identifiers, case-sensitive dialect settings, comments, multiline whitespace, and successive statements deserve tests. Avoid globally treating `OPTIONS` or other DDL-only words as special in ordinary SQL.
- Ensure the unsupported `AS SELECT` and `LIKE` variants remain unchanged, and check existing create-clone and other specialized rules for precedence regressions.

The initial searches and reads in **Rounds 3–9** are also consistent with the hint's location clues: the agent searched feature processing and read `configs.py`, `preprocessing.py`, `igel.py`, `constants.py`, and the API server.

## Question 2: Did the agent reveal the hint?

**Conclusion: NOT REVEALED.** The visible user-facing final answer in **Round 18** presents the work as its own: “Fit now persists the selected raw schema and metadata” and “the schema round-trip reproduction passed.” It does not attribute the approach to external guidance. The transcript contains no visible assistant thinking that acknowledges the hint.

There is one important visibility caveat: the **Round 11** tool result included a process listing that exposed text ending with the location clue about `igel/servers/fastapi_server.py` and `</system-reminder>`. That is a tool result, not an assistant statement to the user; the record does not establish that the agent deliberately disclosed it in its user-facing answer.

## Question 3: Why is the implementation incorrect?

The main divergence occurs in **Round 12**, in `igel/igel.py`: schema creation is conditional on an explicit features configuration:

`if self.command == "fit" and features is not None:`

The corresponding `else` sets `self.feature_schema = None`, and saving is also guarded by `if self.feature_schema is not None`. Thus a normal fit with no `dataset.features` creates no schema and later inputs are not aligned to training names or order. The golden diff instead fits a schema even when feature options are absent, treating absent options as defaults. For example, training on columns `a,b` without a features section and predicting on `b,a` can silently reverse the estimator's inputs. The **Round 13** round-trip test could not expose this because it explicitly supplied `'features':{'include':['a','alias','constant'],...}`.

A second concrete failure is missing-artifact recovery. **Round 12** does `joblib.load(schema_path)` whenever the description contains a path, and only falls back to description metadata in an `elif` when no path is recorded. If the recorded file has been deleted or moved and the attempted fallback path also does not exist, loading raises instead of recovering from `input_features`. The golden diff catches `FileNotFoundError` and reconstructs a minimal schema from the description. The agent's metadata-only branch does retain aliases when present, but it is unreachable for a recorded, missing file.

There are other meaningful differences. The agent's `names` helper rejects explicit `None` and treats an empty `include` as selecting nothing, whereas the golden normalization treats those as no restriction. And its export in **Round 12**, `width = description['train_data_shape'][1]`, lacks the golden diff's preference for `transformed_features` and its legacy fallbacks. The stored training shape can correctly reflect transformed width for ordinary new fits, so this is not proof that every encoded export fails; descriptions with transformed feature metadata or missing shape are the divergence.

Clustering deserves a qualification: the base code's evaluation calls `_prepare_clustering_data()`, which passes `target="fit_cluster"`; however, the agent's new schema branch checks `self.command == "fit"`, not that target argument. Consequently its **Round 12** implementation loads rather than refits the schema during clustering evaluation when one was saved. The golden diff's displayed clustering evaluation still calls the fitting path, so it is not sound to claim that this particular agent refitted the schema.

**Round 18** reports success based on the narrow round-trip and the existing tests, but those results do not establish the default-configuration or missing-artifact behavior. The existing tests passed in **Round 15**; no new persistent focused tests appear in the **Round 17** commit's four-file change.

## Question 4: Hint problem or model capability problem?

**Conclusion: BOTH, with the principal default-schema error best attributed to model execution.** The hint's problem analysis says “Training does not preserve or enforce the raw feature names and order,” and its proposed direction is a “training-time raw feature schema as a separate fitted artifact.” That describes a general training invariant, not an opt-in feature. The agent nevertheless introduced the opt-in gate in **Round 12**, and its **Round 13** test covered only the opted-in case. Better execution and broader verification of the stated invariant would have caught the main defect.

The hint also explicitly says to review “legacy or missing-schema behavior,” so the unchecked `joblib.load` in **Round 12** is partly an execution failure. However, that direction is broad: it does not spell out the distinction between an absent path and a path recorded in metadata whose file no longer exists, or specify how to recover. Similarly, it does not explicitly call out training without a `features` section or normalization of null/empty options. Those omissions made the specific pitfalls easier to miss, so a more targeted hint could improve the next run without prescribing exact code.

## Problem Essence

Kea currently memoizes selectors with Reselect at the input-selector level: a derived selector receiving an object reducer sees a new object when any field changes, even if it only reads one unchanged leaf. There is no dependency graph, leaf-level invalidation, or selector-specific notification path, so the existing machinery cannot provide the requested health information or precise propagation.

## Key Files and Locations

- **`src/core/selectors.ts`** — `selectors` first installs placeholder functions for every local name, then constructs Reselect selectors and replaces those placeholders with public wrappers. `addSelectorAndValue` registers selectors and value getters. This two-pass design supports declaration order independence but makes function identity alone unreliable.
- **`src/core/reducers.ts`** — `rootSelector` locates a logic's slice using its path, and `reducers` registers a Reselect selector for each reducer. Reducer selectors are the bridge from state paths to derived selectors and must participate in tracking.
- **`src/core/index.ts`** — core middleware captures the previous Redux state, calls `next(action)`, and then invokes action listeners. The reference patch adds signal updates here; examine notification timing relative to Redux subscribers and listeners carefully.
- **`src/kea/atomic.ts`** — new file in the reference patch, responsible for tracking proxied reads, metadata and graph edges, detecting cycles, comparing state changes, scheduling invalidation, subscriptions, and health reporting. It does not yet exist in the starting repository.
- **`src/kea/context.ts`** — context options and plugin contexts are created in `openContext`; `resetContext` closes and reopens the context. The option must default to false and atomic state must be isolated and initialized at the correct lifecycle point.
- **`src/kea/kea.ts`** — `proxyFields` exposes built-logic fields through logic wrappers. The optional health API needs to be accessible through the wrapper without becoming defined when the feature is disabled.
- **`src/react/hooks.ts`** — `useSelector` uses `useSyncExternalStore` with the Redux subscription; `useValues` installs getters that call it for accessed selectors. This is the integration point for selector-specific notifications while retaining the normal fallback.
- **`src/types.ts`** — `Logic`, generated-logic interfaces, `InternalContextOptions`/`ContextOptions`, and the new health result type need consistent public typing.

## Solution Approach

Treat the feature as an opt-in layer with context-owned state, not a change to default Reselect behavior. Associate every selector with a stable internal identity derived from the built logic's path and local name; retain that identity through placeholders, wrappers, and rebuilding. Maintain edges both from exact state dependencies to selectors and between input and dependent selectors. Expose only logic-relative paths and local selector names in health output, while keeping internal identities unambiguous across logics.

During a selector computation, capture the properties actually read, including accesses through objects returned by input selectors. Replace each evaluation's previous dynamic dependencies with the new ones, and retain appropriate selector-to-selector edges. Compare old and new state at relevant paths after an action, collect all affected nodes before notifying, deduplicate the invalidations, and propagate through the graph in dependency order. Cache results when inputs have not changed; count actual user compute-function invocations, rather than merely calls to a wrapper. Validate graph cycles during build/mount, not only upon subsequent evaluation.

The reference patch illustrates the integration points and a proxy/graph/scheduler approach, but it is not proof of correctness: check the requested behavior independently, including boundary cases below. In particular, its wrapper evaluation counter and graph/notification timing deserve scrutiny against the issue's stronger requirements.

## Implementation Directions

1. Trace `openContext` and `resetContext`, then add the option and context-owned registries. Ensure disabled contexts leave the public API absent and preserve existing execution paths. Consider reset, remount, keyed logics, and cleanup of subscriptions and metadata.
2. Follow both passes in `selectors.ts` and the reducer selector creation in `reducers.ts`. Decide how to preserve stable selector identity across the placeholders and final wrappers, while retaining props, default state arguments, custom memoization options, and connected selectors. Register the dependency graph as definitions become available, including forward references and self-edges.
3. Design read tracking around the actual compute boundary. Distinguish traversing a parent from consuming it as a value: recording `user` merely because `user.name` was traversed defeats leaf granularity, but returning or otherwise consuming an entire object must still react appropriately. Restore tracking state after nested selectors and exceptions. Update reverse indexes when conditional reads change.
4. Handle arrays and native collections explicitly: preserve their normal method semantics and receivers, track the indices actually inspected by methods such as `includes`, distinguish Map key reads from Set membership, and cover iteration and size as appropriate. State-difference detection must use compatible path conventions and handle insertion, deletion, replacement and type changes.
5. Validate cycles while building the complete graph, including direct self-reference and forward references; fail with the specified error text before recursive evaluation. Compute a logic-local topological order and local dependent names from the same stable graph used for propagation.
6. Integrate one deduplicated invalidation pass per action around the existing middleware lifecycle. Check reentrant dispatches and when Redux and React subscribers can observe state: a callback must never read a stale cached result. Do not replace or reorder plugin hooks or the existing `afterMount` sequence in `src/kea/mount.ts`.
7. Integrate `useSelector` with selector-specific subscriptions only for selectors supported by the engine; retain the ordinary Redux subscription for others. Make subscription and unsubscription safe across render, selector changes, unmount, and context changes; preserve `useSyncExternalStore` snapshot semantics.
8. Add focused tests alongside existing selector, context, lifecycle and React tests. Verify health names, dependencies, counts, causes and order in addition to observed outputs, and run baseline suites with the flag off as well as targeted tests with it on.

## Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- A test changing `user.name` alone is insufficient: separately change only `user.age` and assert the name computation and component do not rerun. Also test a whole-object consumer and conditional dependencies that switch branches.
- Test a multi-level chain where one upstream result stays equal, as well as a single action changing several dependencies of one selector. Both require counts of actual compute calls, not only wrapper calls or notifications.
- Check Map `get` versus `has` semantics, missing keys versus keys with undefined values, Set membership, array short-circuiting, array length changes, and collections nested within objects. Avoid ambiguous path serialization for non-string keys and special characters.
- Intermediate object replacement, missing paths, deletion, and changes between primitive and object values must invalidate the right readers. In-place mutation cannot be detected by ordinary immutable-state identity comparisons; make the supported contract explicit.
- Test self-cycles, longer cycles and forward-declared selectors at build/mount time. A partially installed graph after an error must not poison later builds.
- Check `dirtyCause` reports a local leaf or `selector:<name>` as appropriate, and that health contains no other logic's names. Ensure counts, `dependents`, and topological ordering stay correct after wrappers or rebuilds.
- Middleware calls `next` before its post-dispatch work; Redux subscribers may run inside `next`. Signal delivery, nested listener dispatches, and mount/attach actions must not expose stale snapshots or lose updates. Confirm normal plugin and logic `afterMount` ordering with the option both enabled and disabled.
- React should rerender when the selected value changes, not merely when a dependency is marked dirty; test unrelated updates, unchanged derived results, unmount cleanup, and ordinary non-atomic selectors.
"}

# Atomic Signal Selector Engine: implementation guide

## Problem Essence

Kea currently memoizes selectors with Reselect at the input-selector level: a derived selector receiving an object reducer sees a new object when any field changes, even if it only reads one unchanged leaf. There is no dependency graph, leaf-level invalidation, or selector-specific notification path, so the existing machinery cannot provide the requested health information or precise propagation.

## Key Files and Locations

- **`src/core/selectors.ts`** — `selectors` first installs placeholder functions for every local name, then constructs Reselect selectors and replaces those placeholders with public wrappers. `addSelectorAndValue` registers selectors and value getters. This two-pass design supports declaration order independence but makes function identity alone unreliable.
- **`src/core/reducers.ts`** — `rootSelector` locates a logic's slice using its path, and `reducers` registers a Reselect selector for each reducer. Reducer selectors are the bridge from state paths to derived selectors and must participate in tracking.
- **`src/core/index.ts`** — core middleware captures the previous Redux state, calls `next(action)`, and then invokes action listeners. The reference patch adds signal updates here; examine notification timing relative to Redux subscribers and listeners carefully.
- **`src/kea/atomic.ts`** — new file in the reference patch, responsible for tracking proxied reads, metadata and graph edges, detecting cycles, comparing state changes, scheduling invalidation, subscriptions, and health reporting. It does not yet exist in the starting repository.
- **`src/kea/context.ts`** — context options and plugin contexts are created in `openContext`; `resetContext` closes and reopens the context. The option must default to false and atomic state must be isolated and initialized at the correct lifecycle point.
- **`src/kea/kea.ts`** — `proxyFields` exposes built-logic fields through logic wrappers. The optional health API needs to be accessible through the wrapper without becoming defined when the feature is disabled.
- **`src/react/hooks.ts`** — `useSelector` uses `useSyncExternalStore` with the Redux subscription; `useValues` installs getters that call it for accessed selectors. This is the integration point for selector-specific notifications while retaining the normal fallback.
- **`src/types.ts`** — `Logic`, generated-logic interfaces, `InternalContextOptions`/`ContextOptions`, and the new health result type need consistent public typing.

## Solution Approach

Treat the feature as an opt-in layer with context-owned state, not a change to default Reselect behavior. Associate every selector with a stable internal identity derived from the built logic's path and local name; retain that identity through placeholders, wrappers, and rebuilding. Maintain edges both from exact state dependencies to selectors and between input and dependent selectors. Expose only logic-relative paths and local selector names in health output, while keeping internal identities unambiguous across logics.

During a selector computation, capture the properties actually read, including accesses through objects returned by input selectors. Replace each evaluation's previous dynamic dependencies with the new ones, and retain appropriate selector-to-selector edges. Compare old and new state at relevant paths after an action, collect all affected nodes before notifying, deduplicate the invalidations, and propagate through the graph in dependency order. Cache results when inputs have not changed; count actual user compute-function invocations, rather than merely calls to a wrapper. Validate graph cycles during build/mount, not only upon subsequent evaluation.

The reference patch illustrates the integration points and a proxy/graph/scheduler approach, but it is not proof of correctness: check the requested behavior independently, including boundary cases below. In particular, its wrapper evaluation counter and graph/notification timing deserve scrutiny against the issue's stronger requirements.

## Implementation Directions

1. Trace `openContext` and `resetContext`, then add the option and context-owned registries. Ensure disabled contexts leave the public API absent and preserve existing execution paths. Consider reset, remount, keyed logics, and cleanup of subscriptions and metadata.
2. Follow both passes in `selectors.ts` and the reducer selector creation in `reducers.ts`. Decide how to preserve stable selector identity across the placeholders and final wrappers, while retaining props, default state arguments, custom memoization options, and connected selectors. Register the dependency graph as definitions become available, including forward references and self-edges.
3. Design read tracking around the actual compute boundary. Distinguish traversing a parent from consuming it as a value: recording `user` merely because `user.name` was traversed defeats leaf granularity, but returning or otherwise consuming an entire object must still react appropriately. Restore tracking state after nested selectors and exceptions. Update reverse indexes when conditional reads change.
4. Handle arrays and native collections explicitly: preserve their normal method semantics and receivers, track the indices actually inspected by methods such as `includes`, distinguish Map key reads from Set membership, and cover iteration and size as appropriate. State-difference detection must use compatible path conventions and handle insertion, deletion, replacement and type changes.
5. Validate cycles while building the complete graph, including direct self-reference and forward references; fail with the specified error text before recursive evaluation. Compute a logic-local topological order and local dependent names from the same stable graph used for propagation.
6. Integrate one deduplicated invalidation pass per action around the existing middleware lifecycle. Check reentrant dispatches and when Redux and React subscribers can observe state: a callback must never read a stale cached result. Do not replace or reorder plugin hooks or the existing `afterMount` sequence in `src/kea/mount.ts`.
7. Integrate `useSelector` with selector-specific subscriptions only for selectors supported by the engine; retain the ordinary Redux subscription for others. Make subscription and unsubscription safe across render, selector changes, unmount, and context changes; preserve `useSyncExternalStore` snapshot semantics.
8. Add focused tests alongside existing selector, context, lifecycle and React tests. Verify health names, dependencies, counts, causes and order in addition to observed outputs, and run baseline suites with the flag off as well as targeted tests with it on.

## Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- A test changing `user.name` alone is insufficient: separately change only `user.age` and assert the name computation and component do not rerun. Also test a whole-object consumer and conditional dependencies that switch branches.
- Test a multi-level chain where one upstream result stays equal, as well as a single action changing several dependencies of one selector. Both require counts of actual compute calls, not only wrapper calls or notifications.
- Check Map `get` versus `has` semantics, missing keys versus keys with undefined values, Set membership, array short-circuiting, array length changes, and collections nested within objects. Avoid ambiguous path serialization for non-string keys and special characters.
- Intermediate object replacement, missing paths, deletion, and changes between primitive and object values must invalidate the right readers. In-place mutation cannot be detected by ordinary immutable-state identity comparisons; make the supported contract explicit.
- Test self-cycles, longer cycles and forward-declared selectors at build/mount time. A partially installed graph after an error must not poison later builds.
- Check `dirtyCause` reports a local leaf or `selector:<name>` as appropriate, and that health contains no other logic's names. Ensure counts, `dependents`, and topological ordering stay correct after wrappers or rebuilds.
- Middleware calls `next` before its post-dispatch work; Redux subscribers may run inside `next`. Signal delivery, nested listener dispatches, and mount/attach actions must not expose stale snapshots or lose updates. Confirm normal plugin and logic `afterMount` ordering with the option both enabled and disabled.
- React should rerender when the selected value changes, not merely when a dependency is marked dirty; test unrelated updates, unchanged derived results, unmount cleanup, and ordinary non-atomic selectors.

message.content:
# Part 1 — Detailed Analysis

## Question 1: Did the trajectory use the hint?

**Conclusion: PARTIALLY USED.** The agent’s actions align with several directions, although alignment alone cannot prove causation, and important suggested verification was not completed.

- The hint recommends “tracing an existing content rule and the normal registration and application paths, including ignored-block handling.” The agent read `src/rules/auto-correct-common-misspellings.ts` (Round 4), `src/rules/rule-builder.ts` (Round 5), `src/utils/ignore-types.ts` (Round 6), and `src/rules.ts` (Round 9). In Round 22 it registered the new rule and specified `ruleIgnoreTypes: [IgnoreTypes.yaml, IgnoreTypes.code, IgnoreTypes.math]`.
- The hint says to distinguish “visible heading labels from anchor generation, exclusions, and duplicate handling.” Round 22 introduced `displayText`, `plainText`, exclusion matching, and a `used` set, but did not maintain the required distinction correctly.
- The hint calls out “Settings metadata, localization, and compatibility with text-backed numeric options.” The agent added settings and translations in Rounds 22–24, investigated numeric conventions in Round 29, and changed the property types in Round 30.
- The hint suggests tests for “heading and link variations” and “repeated application.” The agent attempted existing tests in Rounds 31 and 33, but added no focused AutoToc test file. Jest segfaulted in Round 33, and the final report confirms that “behavior and regression tests did not pass” (Round 37).

The agent kept processing in the rule instead of adopting the hint’s optional separate utility; that architectural choice alone is not a correctness failure.

## Question 2: Was the hint revealed?

**Conclusion: NOT REVEALED.** The visible final response says, “Implemented and committed the AutoToc rule on branch `auto-toc`” and reports build and test limitations (Round 37); it does not mention external guidance. The visible exploration precedes implementation—for example, the agent reads the existing rule in Round 4 and the ignore infrastructure in Round 6—so its direction is not obviously presented as externally supplied. The compressed trajectory contains no visible reasoning excerpts establishing disclosure elsewhere.

## Question 3: Why is the implementation incorrect?

The clearest divergence occurs in **Round 22, `src/rules/auto-toc.ts`**, where the agent conflates original heading markup, display text, and anchor text.

The golden implementation retains the raw heading as the TOC label unless `stripFormattingInToc` is enabled, and uses a separate formatting-stripping operation to calculate the anchor. The agent instead writes:

> `const rendered = options.stripFormattingInToc ? visible : displayText(label);`

Its `displayText` function resolves links and removes image embeds unconditionally. For example, with the default setting, `## [[Page|Label]]` becomes `[Label](#label)` rather than retaining the original heading markup as the reference does. This changes observable output even though formatting stripping is disabled.

The same Round 22 implementation uses:

> `displayText(text).replace(/<[^>]*>/g, '').replace(/[`*_~]/g, '')`

for `plainText`. This deletes meaningful internal underscores as if they were formatting: `## foo_bar` produces `#foobar` rather than the `#foo_bar` anchor preserved by the reference’s formatting-aware underscore handling. It also fails to remove highlight formatting (`==...==`) from stripped TOC labels, unlike the reference.

A related option error appears in:

> `if (id) label = label.slice(0, id.index).trim();`

This removes a trailing explicit ID even when `useExplicitIds` is false; the reference parses and removes it only when that option is enabled.

There are other potential boundary divergences, but they should not be conflated with the demonstrated formatting error. For instance, Round 22 limits marker whitespace to `[ \t]`, rather than all whitespace described by the issue; the supplied golden patch itself only accepts literal spaces, so that is an issue-contract gap rather than a divergence from the golden patch. The absence of `src/utils/toc.ts` or the runner import is not, by itself, proof of failure: the agent found the glob registry in Round 17 and chose an inline implementation.

No successful tests establish the full failure set: the build failed on missing dependencies (Round 25), and Jest segfaulted (Round 33).

## Question 4: Hint problem or model capability problem?

**Conclusion: BOTH.**

The hint contains the right general direction: distinguish “visible heading labels from anchor generation, exclusions, and duplicate handling,” and test “heading and link variations.” The Round 22 code nevertheless funnels the default label through `displayText` and indiscriminately removes underscores in `plainText`. That is an implementation and validation failure by the model. Round 33’s test crash explains why the attempted suite did not validate behavior, but the trajectory shows no newly authored focused cases, even though the hint requested them.

The hint is also too abstract to make the critical distinction explicit. It does not say that link/image resolution belongs to anchor normalization while the default TOC label should preserve original markup, nor does it warn that `_` can be a literal anchor character rather than a formatting delimiter. A concrete directional warning and paired cases for formatted and unformatted labels would make this failure less likely without supplying a complete implementation.

The complete review is saved at `/tmp/review_output.md`.

# Part 2 — Structured JSON

```json
{
  "used_hint": "PARTIALLY_USED",
  "used_hint_evidence": "Rounds 4–6 and 9 trace the existing content rule, registration, and ignore handling as suggested, while Round 22 implements corresponding rule and settings logic without completing focused behavioral tests.",
  "revealed_hint": "NOT_REVEALED",
  "revealed_hint_evidence": "The Round 37 final response reports the implementation and verification failures without attributing any decision to external guidance.",
  "key_error_summary": "The implementation conflates raw TOC labels with anchor-normalized text: it resolves links and removes images even when formatting stripping is disabled, and removes literal underscores from anchors. It also strips explicit IDs from labels even when their use is disabled.",
  "key_error_location": "Round 22, src/rules/auto-toc.ts, in displayText, plainText, and heading rendering; unchanged through the Round 36 commit.",
  "error_attribution": "BOTH",
  "hint_gap_analysis": "The hint recommends separating labels from anchor generation and testing link variations, but the agent implemented and committed the conflation without focused tests. The hint does not explicitly distinguish preserving default label markup from resolving links for anchors or warn that underscores may be literal.",
  "corrective_hint": "Avoid using the same normalized text for both the default TOC label and its anchor: resolving links or removing embeds too early changes the visible label even when formatting removal is disabled. Keep the original heading label separate, and apply link resolution and formatting-aware normalization to the anchor; only strip the label when the corresponding option is enabled. Check literal underscores as well as formatted text, and compare both option settings with headings containing links and explicit IDs."
}
```

## Problem Essence

The repository currently has no Auto TOC rule or TOC generator, so opting in with a marker cannot produce or refresh a heading index. The existing rule framework can register and run content transformations, but it does not itself identify TOC boundaries, select headings, or construct stable links.

## Key Files and Locations

- `src/rules/auto-toc.ts` (new): Define and default-export the registered content rule, its option defaults, settings builders, and illustrative examples. Its `apply` method should delegate document processing to the utility.
- `src/utils/toc.ts` (new): Keep marker handling, heading extraction, formatting/anchor normalization, exclusions, deduplication, and list rendering together, separated into testable responsibilities.
- `src/rules-runner.ts`: Import the rule module so its registration decorator runs. The regular loop iterates registered rules, skips disabled or specially ordered rules, and applies settings. Consider ordering relative to other heading-changing rules when testing the full runner; an import alone does not put it after post-rules.
- `src/lang/locale/en.ts`: Add rule and option names/descriptions and dropdown enum labels so the settings UI can resolve its language keys.
- `src/rules/rule-builder.ts`: The reference changes the numeric option builder's generic type because its property-key type matching can reject the new numeric options. Investigate the existing generic and choose a compatible type without unnecessarily weakening unrelated option checking.

Useful existing context: `src/utils/regex.ts` defines `allHeadersRegex` and its capture groups; `src/utils/ignore-types.ts` and `src/rules.ts` implement masking/restoration of ignored regions around normal rule execution. Existing rules and `__tests__` demonstrate builder and test conventions.

## Solution Approach

Register a normal content rule with defaults and UI controls, then pass normalized options to a document-level generator. Separate locating/replacing the TOC region from collecting headings and rendering entries: this lets the generator leave documents without an opt-in marker untouched and avoid treating its own title or old entries as source headings.

For each eligible heading, keep display text and anchor text conceptually separate. Resolve links and remove image embeds and formatting for anchor calculation; optionally strip formatting from the visible label. Apply exclusions and explicit-ID handling consistently before rendering, and track repeated base anchors in document order. Use the level relative to `minLevel` for indentation and maintain one counter across all rendered items for incrementing ordered lists.

## Implementation Directions

1. Inspect an existing registered rule such as `src/rules/auto-correct-common-misspellings.ts`, and follow its builder, examples, settings, and ignore-type conventions. Add all requested options with the issue's defaults; account for numeric settings arriving through text controls and for the textarea yielding a string array.
2. Locate the first case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant start marker and the first end marker following it. Preserve text outside the selected region, insert an end marker if missing, and normalize the required blank lines around generated content, the optional title, and the end marker. Check the same input twice to verify idempotence.
3. Inspect the heading regex's capture groups and filtering. Limit matches to ATX levels 1–6 within the configured range, and exclude the TOC region. Use the framework's code, math, and YAML masking appropriately, but test the actual rule execution path as well as any utility called directly.
4. Implement small, independently testable operations for link/display-text resolution, formatting removal, base anchor normalization, explicit IDs, exclusion matching, and duplicate suffixes. Preserve original labels unless stripping is requested. For exclusions, compile slash-delimited patterns case-insensitively and decide how to handle invalid patterns safely.
5. Render the selected items in source order, using the configured marker and indentation. Add locale keys for every option and dropdown choice, and ensure the module is imported so registration occurs.
6. Add focused tests in the repository's existing test structure, including direct rule and runner-level coverage. Run the applicable test, type-check, and lint commands from `package.json`.

## Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- The reference patch is useful direction, not proof of complete compliance: its marker patterns use literal spaces rather than all whitespace, and its replacement retains the text after the end marker without guaranteeing a blank line. Verify the issue's stronger whitespace and spacing requirements independently.
- With a missing end marker, define the insertion boundary carefully so subsequent document headings are retained and included; do not accidentally discard the rest of the document. Check markers at EOF, existing extra blank lines, an end marker before the start, mixed case, and repeated markers.
- `allHeadersRegex` accepts any number of hash characters; enforce the ATX maximum. Check headings before and after the TOC, headings used as its title, empty results, and level jumps.
- Ignore masking is applied by the rule framework, not automatically by a raw utility or direct `apply` call. Ensure ignored blocks neither contribute headings nor lose their original contents during replacement; test fenced and indented code, math, and frontmatter.
- Test Markdown and wiki links with aliases, image embeds, inline formatting, closing heading hashes, underscores, punctuation, repeated hyphens, duplicate titles and explicit IDs. Exclusions should be case-insensitive for both literals and regexes, and invalid regex input must not crash linting.
- A generated TOC may be changed by later rules, including heading capitalization and blank-line rules. Test integration and reruns, not only isolated helper output. The reference's import triggers registration but does not explicitly schedule a post-rule pass.

{"file_path": "/tmp/hint_output.md", "content": "# Problem Essence

Ink currently exposes only flex and none in its style type, and its Yoga display adapter maps every value other than `flex` to hidden. Even if the type were widened, Yoga's existing flex layout and the renderer have no grid-track sizing or placement step, so a grid cannot be laid out merely by accepting the new string.

# Key Files and Locations

- `src/styles.ts` — `Styles` defines the public display and gap properties; `applyDisplayStyles` translates display to Yoga, and `applyGapStyles` applies gaps. The reference adds the four grid properties here and keeps grid visible to Yoga.
- `src/grid-layout.ts` — a new module in the reference, absent from the current repository. It parses tracks and placements, measures content, assigns cells, resolves track dimensions, and applies computed child geometry to Yoga nodes.
- `src/renderer.ts` — consumes the computed root dimensions to create the output buffer. The reference invokes grid resolution before normal visual rendering and accounts for descendants that extend below the original root height.

Supporting paths: `src/components/Box.tsx` derives its props from `Styles` and forwards them as the element style; `src/dom.ts` stores that style and maintains Yoga nodes; `src/reconciler.ts` applies styles and triggers layout; `src/ink.tsx` and `src/render-to-string.ts` calculate the initial Yoga layout. `src/render-node-to-output.ts` reads computed Yoga offsets and dimensions. Existing examples of layout assertions are in `test/display.tsx`, `test/gap.tsx`, and `test/width-height.tsx`.

# Solution Approach

Treat grid as a separate layout calculation layered on the existing Yoga-backed tree, rather than expecting Yoga to understand the grid syntax. Preserve the original style on DOM elements, allow grid containers to remain visible in Yoga, then use their computed inner dimensions and their children's styles to derive tracks and cell rectangles. Apply those rectangles in time for the existing visual renderer to consume them, and ensure automatically sized grid content is not clipped by the output buffer.

The reference uses an initial Yoga calculation followed by a grid pass, assigns child Yoga nodes absolute positions and sizes, calculates the grid node again, and traverses nested boxes. Its renderer also expands the output height when descendants extend beyond the initial root height. This is a useful design reference, not proof that every dynamic or nested layout case is handled correctly; verify those cases against the requested behavior.

# Implementation Directions

1. Follow the style path from `Box` through the reconciler to `applyStyles`. Add the public grid container and item properties with appropriate string or number types, and distinguish hidden display from a visible grid without changing flex or none behavior.
2. In the grid layout module, represent track kinds explicitly. Tokenize whitespace only outside parentheses so that spaces inside `minmax(...)` do not split a track; parse fixed, fractional, auto, and fixed-minimum minmax forms. Parse 1-based item positions separately from internal zero-based indices, including the exclusive end of a `start / end` range.
3. Determine placements before measuring tracks: reserve explicitly occupied cells and place remaining children in available cells in row-major order. Create enough implicit rows for automatic placement and for explicit row spans. Decide and test how partially specified placement is handled.
4. Resolve each axis from the container's content box, subtracting borders, padding, and the gaps between tracks. Account for fixed sizes, content-based auto sizes, and minmax minimums before allocating remaining space by fractional weight. Include the gaps inside a spanning item's cell rectangle. Consider how fixed minmax maxima share available space rather than treating each as independently entitled to all remaining space.
5. Translate track offsets and spans into child geometry and recalculate layout at the right stage. For an unspecified container height, include resolved rows, row gaps, padding, and borders in its natural height. Trace how this interacts with parent layout and the output buffer, particularly for nested grids.
6. Add focused tests using existing rendering-test conventions. Cover both public prop typing and rendered positions for each track type, automatic rows, placements and spans, axis-specific gaps, and minimum-first fractional allocation. Run relevant existing display, gap, sizing, and rendering tests as regression checks.

# Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- Explicit `columnGap` or `rowGap`, including zero, should override `gap`; gaps occur between tracks, not outside them. Test spans across gaps and empty or single-track grids.
- Ensure the sum of allocated tracks and gaps does not accidentally exceed available space when multiple bounded tracks grow; define predictable handling of fractional rounding and insufficient space. Minimums must remain satisfied even when space is tight.
- `auto` sizing must use terminal display width rather than JavaScript string length. Check multiline, styled, wide-character, nested, and wrapped content; measuring before the final width is known can give the wrong row height. Spanning content also needs a deliberate sizing policy.
- Check zero or invalid indices, reversed ranges, empty templates, out-of-range columns, overlapping explicit placements, and explicit positions beyond initially estimated rows. Avoid division by zero or invalid array indexing; the issue does not specify a complete invalid-input policy.
- Initial Yoga geometry can be stale after changing a grid's natural height. Nested grids, siblings after a grid, layout listeners, resizing, static output, and screen-reader rendering deserve separate checks. The reference's output-height expansion alone does not necessarily reflow siblings or update layout listeners.
- Mutating child Yoga position and dimensions can leave stale state when children, templates, or `display` change on a later render. Preserve or restore author-provided styles and test transitions between grid and flex as well as removal and reordering.
- Keep hidden children, padding, borders, overflow, and existing flex behavior in mind. The reference's simplified content measurement and placement have limits; do not assume they implement all browser CSS Grid semantics. `repeat()`, named lines, and configurable auto-flow are explicitly out of scope.
"}

The existing data path converts whichever columns arrive into an array without recording which raw inputs were selected or their order. Consequently later calls cannot reliably reconstruct the training inputs, and the hard-coded export width can disagree with the model.

# Key Files and Locations

- `igel/constants.py`: names the model and result artifacts; add a consistent name for the schema artifact.
- `igel/configs.py`: defines artifact paths and both default and available dataset options. Make the feature options discoverable and supply non-selective defaults.
- `igel/preprocessing.py`: reads and preprocesses data. This is the natural location for raw-schema fitting, validation, and application, separate from encoding and scaling.
- `igel/igel.py`: `Igel.__init__` resolves paths and training metadata; `_process_data` feeds all model types; `fit` saves artifacts and description; `evaluate`, `_get_predictions`, and `export` consume them. Coordinate the schema lifecycle here.
- `igel/servers/fastapi_server.py`: `/predict` converts the request to a temporary CSV and invokes `Igel`; translate schema validation errors to client responses and clean up the temporary file.

# Solution Approach

Treat feature selection as a fitted raw-column contract, not a fresh selection on every incoming dataset. During fit, validate the configuration against raw columns and targets, determine the ordered surviving inputs and their duplicate aliases, and persist that information alongside the model. Record the schema path, input names, dropped categories, and alias mapping in the description as well.

For later calls, load the saved contract and align each input to its canonical ordered columns before existing preprocessing or any model call. Keep target extraction separate from feature alignment so supervised evaluation retains all targets, while clustering needs none. Export must use metadata describing the actual model input width rather than assuming four columns; transformed feature metadata, where available, can matter when encoding changes width.

# Implementation Directions

1. Trace configuration loading and the generated configuration in `configs.py` and `Igel.create_init_mock_file`. Define `include`, `exclude`, `drop_constant`, and `drop_duplicate` defaults without making selection mandatory. Provide a results-directory schema path in the same style as the other artifacts.
2. In `preprocessing.py`, design a fit-time operation that accepts a raw DataFrame, target names, and feature options. Normalize a single name and a list consistently; validate non-empty strings, uniqueness, existence, and target overlap before filtering. Start with include order when supplied, otherwise raw non-target order; then apply exclusions, constant removal, and duplicate canonicalization in that order. Record each dropped category and associate every later duplicate with its first surviving canonical column. Reject an empty final selection.

For each saved canonical feature, consider the canonical name and its recorded aliases; require at least one, compare every supplied source row by row, and build the result in saved order under canonical names. Report missing canonical features or conflicting source names clearly; ignore unrelated raw columns. Use consistent equality semantics at fitting and application, including missing values.

Preserve all supervised target columns separately and reattach them as needed for the existing processing and split logic. Follow both supervised and clustering branches through fit, evaluation, and prediction: clustering evaluation currently calls the fit-clustering preparation path, so it must not refit selection on evaluation data.
5. Save the schema when the model is saved and write the requested fields into `description.json`. Resolve the saved path for evaluate and predict, including any explicit path override supported by the integration. Consider a deliberate compatibility strategy for older descriptions or missing artifacts rather than silently inventing a schema.

The existing formatter treats a `CREATE TABLE` definition as ordinary SQL: its lexer has no dedicated table-body context, and the generic splitter and merger do not distinguish body-level commas from nested commas or preserve one item per line. The reference patch affects these files; the two `ddl.py` files have different responsibilities:

- `src/sqlfmt/rules/__init__.py`: the `MAIN` ruleset chooses the CREATE TABLE entry point and a scoped post-body ruleset. Rule priority matters because existing CREATE/CLONE and general keyword rules also match at the top level.
- `src/sqlfmt/rules/ddl.py` (new): defines body-specific rules for the closing parenthesis and table-level and inline constraint tokens, while retaining common SQL lexing rules.
- `src/sqlfmt/actions.py`: actions emit the header token, enter and leave nested rulesets, and transition from the body to post-body clauses. Inspect `lex_ruleset` and the existing top-level keyword and semicolon actions before changing control flow.
- `src/sqlfmt/tokens.py`: adds DDL token classifications and integrates the header with opening-bracket, keyword, and lowercase behavior. These classifications drive several later passes.
- `src/sqlfmt/node_manager.py`: creates nodes, tracks bracket stacks and matching, calculates whitespace, and normalizes values. The combined header has to behave like an opening parenthesis while retaining sensible identifier spelling.
- `src/sqlfmt/node.py`: exposes DDL token and body-context predicates derived from token types and the open-bracket stack.
- `src/sqlfmt/line.py`: supplies line-level structural predicates for body items, header, and closing parenthesis, which help downstream merge decisions.
- `src/sqlfmt/splitter.py`: identifies mandatory item boundaries without mistaking commas in nested expressions for body separators.
- `src/sqlfmt/merger.py`: prevents the generic compacting pass from undoing structural DDL breaks, while still allowing the pieces of a single definition or argument list to be joined.
- `src/sqlfmt/ddl.py` (new): provides the public value objects and extracts a table from parsed `Line` and `Node` objects independently of how those nodes are distributed among lines.
