# Auto TOC: implementation guide

## Problem Essence

The current repository has no Auto TOC rule or TOC generation utility, so there is nothing that recognizes the opt-in markers and turns document headings into a maintained list. Adding only a text formatter would also leave it disconnected from the rule registry, settings, localization, and the existing mechanism for excluding protected Markdown regions.

## Key Files and Locations

- **`src/rules/auto-toc.ts` (new):** Define the default-exported, registered content rule, its option defaults and settings controls, and representative examples. Its application method should delegate the document transformation to the utility.
- **`src/utils/toc.ts` (new):** House marker handling, heading collection, display and anchor normalization, exclusions, deduplication, and list generation. Keeping these concerns separate makes the transformation independently testable.
- **`src/rules-runner.ts`:** Import the rule so its registration decorator runs. The runner iterates registered, enabled regular rules; an unimported decorated class will not register itself.
- **`src/lang/locale/en.ts`:** Add the rule and option names and descriptions, plus the dropdown enum labels used by the builders. `LanguageStringKey` and the UI rely on these keys.
- **`src/rules/rule-builder.ts`:** Inspect `NumberOptionBuilder` and its generic option-key constraints. The reference loosens its value type to accommodate numeric option properties; consider the type-safety implications and verify existing numeric options still work.
- **Related existing code:** `src/rules.ts` wraps rule application with ignore handling; `src/utils/ignore-types.ts` implements it. `src/utils/regex.ts` exports `allHeadersRegex`, whose capture groups separate heading level, text, and optional closing hashes. Existing rules such as `ordered-list-style.ts` demonstrate registration, options, examples, and ignored regions.

## Solution Approach

Connect a small rule adapter to a document-level generator. The adapter supplies defaults and option builders, declares code, math, and YAML as ignored types, and lets the existing rule machinery protect those spans before the generator runs. Understand the difference between calling the builder’s `apply` directly and calling the registered `Rule.apply`: the latter performs the ignore wrapping.

In the utility, first establish whether the document opts in and locate the first start marker and first subsequent end marker. Collect eligible headings outside the existing TOC, normalize their labels and anchors, filter exclusions, and render entries in document order. Finally, replace only the intended region—or insert an end marker when missing—while preserving surrounding document content and enforcing the requested blank lines. A second run should not change the result.

## Implementation Directions

1. Study an existing `RuleBuilder` rule and `RuleBuilder.buildRuleOptions`: settings use localized, hyphenated configuration keys, but the typed options object uses property names. Define all requested defaults, dropdowns, numeric and text controls, booleans, and the newline-separated exclusion control. Convert numeric settings at the boundary because number controls are implemented as text options.
2. Trace `Rule.apply` and the ignore utilities before choosing where heading detection runs. Ensure code, math, and YAML do not contribute headings or accidental markers, and test the public registered-rule path as well as any utility-level API.
3. Match marker case and whitespace flexibly, selecting the first start and only an end after that start. Treat an absent start as an exact no-op. When an end is absent, insert it without discarding the remaining document. Preserve unrelated markers and content.
4. Use the existing ATX heading regex as a starting point, checking its capture groups and level bounds. Exclude headings within the TOC itself, including a heading used as the optional title. Compute indentation relative to the configured minimum level, not the preceding item’s level.
5. Keep label rendering distinct from anchor generation: resolve wiki and Markdown links to display text, remove image embeds before resolving links, strip formatting for anchors, and optionally strip it from visible labels. Handle trailing heading hashes and optional explicit IDs at the appropriate stage. Normalize and deduplicate anchors consistently in document order.
6. Compile exclusions once per generation: compare literals case-insensitively and recognize slash-delimited case-insensitive regular expressions. Decide safely how invalid regex input should behave rather than allowing a settings typo to crash linting.
7. Render the selected bullet marker or ordered marker; for incrementing ordered lists, count across all emitted items, including nested ones. Add examples and focused tests for both the utility and registry/settings integration, then run the project’s relevant test and type-check commands.

## Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- The reference is a design aid, not proof of full compliance: its marker patterns use literal spaces rather than all whitespace, and its reconstruction does not itself guarantee a blank line after an end marker. Check the issue’s stronger requirements independently.
- When no end marker exists, distinguish the insertion point from the region to exclude: headings after the start still need to be collected and retained. With an existing end, old TOC headings must not appear in the new list.
- Test empty headings and results, a title with no eligible entries, markers adjacent to text or end-of-file, case variants, tabs, multiple markers, and repeated execution. Avoid adding or removing unrelated content when normalizing spacing.
- Test levels at and outside both bounds, skipped levels, nested indentation, and numbering after exclusions. `allHeadersRegex` can match more than six `#` characters, so enforce the requested range.
- Test duplicate normalized anchors, explicit IDs, link aliases, images, punctuation, underscores, and trailing hashes. Consider collisions between a generated suffix and another heading’s base anchor, and how excluded or out-of-range headings affect anchor numbering.
- The text-area builder splits stored strings into arrays; direct typed options and settings-derived options may take different paths. Check both, especially empty arrays and invalid regexes.
- Ignore wrappers restore protected text after transformation. Verify headings and markers around protected spans rather than assuming a raw utility call provides the same protection as the registered rule.

The complete guide was written to `/tmp/hint_output.md`. No branch, source changes, or commit were made because this guidance stage is read-only.

The complete guide is saved at `/tmp/hint_output.md`.

# Problem Essence

The current data path turns whichever columns happen to arrive into a positional NumPy array, after removing targets only for supervised training and evaluation. It neither applies `dataset.features` nor preserves a raw-column contract, so later inputs can silently change order or width; errors are also logged and swallowed before callers can report them.

# Key Files and Locations

- **`igel/configs.py`**: Central results paths and both default and available dataset options. Expose the schema artifact and feature-selection options here.
- **`igel/constants.py`**: Shared artifact filenames, including the new schema filename used alongside the model and description.
- **`igel/preprocessing.py`**: Existing DataFrame reading, encoding, imputation, and scaling helpers. This is a natural location for fitting and applying a reusable raw feature schema and validating its options.
- **`igel/igel.py`**: Initialization chooses paths and loads training metadata; `_process_data` feeds all model types; `fit` saves artifacts and description; `evaluate`, prediction, and `export` consume them. Trace clustering separately: its evaluation currently calls the same preparation method as clustering fit.
- **`igel/servers/fastapi_server.py`**: `/predict` converts request data to CSV and invokes `Igel`. It must translate schema-validation failures to HTTP responses and clean up the temporary file.

# Solution Approach

Treat feature selection as a fitted raw-data contract, distinct from later encoding and scaling. During fit, derive an ordered canonical feature list and record exclusions, constants, duplicate aliases, and configuration; save the contract with the model and summarize it in `description.json`. On every later input, load that contract and construct the canonical ordered frame before preprocessing or a model call, rather than re-discovering features from new data.

Keep target extraction separate from feature selection so all targets remain available for supervised evaluation without becoming model inputs. Clustering has no targets, but must use the same fit-versus-transform distinction. Persisted metadata also gives export the correct model input width instead of its present hard-coded four; prefer a recorded transformed width where available because encoding can change dimensionality, then use appropriate recorded raw features or training shape as fallback.

# Implementation Directions

1. Follow path initialization in `Igel.__init__`, `_save_model`, and the construction of `fit_description`. Add a consistently resolved schema path and artifact serialization, create its parent as needed, and record `feature_schema_path`, `input_features`, `dropped_features`, and `duplicate_feature_aliases` as JSON-compatible metadata. Consider how explicit paths and a description loaded from another results directory interact, and how older descriptions or missing artifacts should behave.

2. In preprocessing, normalize a single name or list, validate non-empty unique names, and reject unknown or target columns. Start from the requested include order, or all raw non-target columns if no include is specified; apply exclusion, then constant removal, then duplicate removal. Record dropped names under the three required keys and map each first surviving canonical column to every later duplicate alias. Reject an empty final selection.

3. Build the transformation around the saved canonical order. For each canonical name, look for it and all recorded aliases; accept any present source, compare all present sources across every row, and report conflicting column names. Collect missing canonical names for a useful error, ignore unrelated extra columns, and emit columns in training order. Use consistent equality semantics for fitting and inference, including missing values.

4. Integrate this immediately after reading raw data and before encoding, missing-value handling, scaling, or conversion to arrays. Preserve targets for the existing supervised preprocessing and splitting paths; never require targets for prediction. Ensure clustering evaluation transforms using the fitted schema instead of fitting a fresh one. Check both single- and multi-target paths.

5. Trace exception handling from `_process_data` through `evaluate` and `_get_predictions`: validation failures must propagate rather than become `None` or an unrelated failure. At the HTTP boundary, convert schema-related `ValueError` to a 400 JSON detail while retaining temporary-file cleanup. Ensure evaluation honors the requested model path as well as the relevant description and schema paths.

6. Replace export’s fixed input width with a value derived from training description metadata, taking account of transformed features versus raw inputs and compatibility with existing descriptions. Test using models with widths other than four.

# Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- Include order determines which duplicate is canonical; exclusions and constants must be processed before duplicate detection. A duplicate list may contain multiple aliases, and alias-only input must still produce the canonical column name.
- Compare every supplied duplicate source row-wise, not just the first row or the column set. Check missing values consistently and name conflicting sources in the error. Ignore extras, but report all missing required canonical features.
- Validate each include/exclude option independently, including repeated names, whitespace-only names, targets, and unknown names; an exclusion can remove all candidates, as can constant or duplicate filtering. Keep all three dropped-feature lists even when empty.
- Do not accidentally treat supervised targets as feature candidates or lose multiple target columns while reconstructing the frame. Check clustering fit, evaluation, and prediction separately.
- Raw schema alignment alone does not persist fitted encoders, imputers, or scalers: the existing helpers fit anew on each dataset, and one-hot encoding can alter transformed width. Avoid claiming that raw schema persistence solves those separate preprocessing consistency limitations.
- Exercise fit artifacts and metadata, reordered and extra columns, alias-only and conflicting inputs, missing features, invalid configurations, HTTP 400 responses, and export width. Check error propagation, not only logged messages.

# Grid layout: implementation guide

## Problem Essence

Ink currently exposes only flex and none as display styles, and its Yoga-backed layout path has no grid track sizing or placement pass. Simply adding `grid` to the type is insufficient: the existing display mapping sends every non-flex value to Yoga's hidden state, and the renderer relies on Yoga's computed geometry and output dimensions.

## Key Files and Locations

- **`src/styles.ts`** — The `Styles` type near `display` defines the public style API, and `applyDisplayStyles` maps it to Yoga. The existing gap properties and `applyGapStyles` show shorthand and per-axis behavior. The reference changes this file to expose grid templates and item placement and keep grid nodes visible to Yoga.
- **`src/grid-layout.ts` (new in the reference)** — The reference isolates parsing, content measurement, placement, track resolution, and application of computed item geometry in a grid-specific layout pass. It traverses the DOM to find grid containers; this file does not exist in the starting repository.
- **`src/renderer.ts`** — The normal rendering branch constructs an `Output` from the root's computed size and then draws the DOM. The reference invokes grid resolution before allocating the output and accounts for descendant bottoms when choosing output height; the screen-reader branch returns earlier and uses a different rendering path.

Related data flow worth tracing: `src/components/Box.tsx` derives its props from `Styles` and forwards style to `ink-box`; `src/reconciler.ts` stores styles on DOM nodes and applies Yoga styles, then invokes layout on commit. `src/dom.ts` owns the DOM/Yoga tree and text measurement. Both `src/ink.tsx` and `src/render-to-string.ts` calculate the root Yoga layout before calling the renderer. `src/render-node-to-output.ts` consumes computed positions and sizes.

## Solution Approach

Keep Yoga responsible for the initial container geometry and ordinary flex layout, while adding a separate grid-specific pass that reads the retained DOM styles. Once the container dimensions are known, parse its tracks, place children, resolve track dimensions, and translate the resulting cells into Yoga child geometry; recalculate layout before drawing. The reference uses absolutely positioned Yoga children for this bridge, and adjusts an auto-height grid and the output canvas to make newly created rows visible.

The pieces depend on one another: placement determines which content contributes to auto tracks and how many implicit rows exist; track sizing determines positions and spans; the renderer must see the resulting geometry and a canvas large enough to draw it. The reference is an implementation direction, not a complete CSS Grid specification; verify behavior against the issue rather than assuming all browser grid semantics.

## Implementation Directions

1. Extend the style interface with the two templates and two item placement properties, and accept grid as a display value. Trace how `Box` passes those properties through the reconciler to `node.style`. In the display adapter, distinguish hiding from the visible layout modes so Yoga does not discard a grid subtree.
2. Build a small representation of fixed, fractional, auto, and min/max tracks. Tokenize at whitespace outside parentheses, since a `minmax` argument can contain spaces. Parse placement into zero-based starts and spans, interpreting the end line as exclusive.
3. Determine explicit placements and mark occupied cells before placing the remaining children in row-major order. Create implicit auto rows as needed, including enough rows for spans or explicit placements. Decide how to handle an item with only one axis specified and test that behavior deliberately.
4. Resolve each axis using the container's content-box space: subtract borders, padding, and gaps, account for fixed and content-sized tracks and minimums, then share remaining space by fractional weight. For a fractional `minmax` maximum, preserve its minimum before distributing growth. Use the existing text measurement helpers for content-sized tracks and consider the effects of wrapping and child dimensions.
5. Derive item offsets and sizes from preceding tracks and intervening gaps, including gaps inside a span. Apply them to the Yoga nodes and recalculate the relevant layout. For an unspecified container height, consider how implicit row sizes contribute to its height and how that change propagates to ancestors and output allocation.
6. Add focused tests alongside `test/gap.tsx`, `test/display.tsx`, and `test/render-to-string.tsx`, using visible output and, where appropriate, layout metrics. Run the project's typecheck, lint, and relevant AVA tests after implementation; also check live rendering and rerenders, not just an initial string render.

## Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- Per-axis gaps should override the shorthand, including an explicit zero; subtract only the gaps between tracks and include internal gaps in a spanning item's size.
- Test mixed fixed, auto, and unequal `fr` tracks, multiple fractional `minmax` minimums, insufficient available space, fixed maximums, fractional rounding, and both axes. Avoid allocating the same remaining space more than once when multiple fixed maximums grow.
- Test omitted row templates, more children than explicit rows, occupied cells, spans, and 1-based line boundaries. Empty or malformed templates and zero columns need safe handling rather than division by zero or nonterminating placement.
- Intrinsic text width is not necessarily wrapped height; nested boxes, borders, padding, and multi-line or wide-character text complicate auto measurement. Spanning children need an explicit sizing policy.
- Borders and padding affect both available content space and coordinates. Check nested grids and sibling layout, fixed versus auto heights, clipping, static output, and screen-reader output separately: increasing the output canvas alone does not necessarily update ancestor Yoga geometry.
- Yoga mutations persist across renders. Check changing templates, removing or reordering children, switching grid back to flex or none, and restoring user-provided positions and dimensions; otherwise stale absolute positioning or grid-computed sizes can leak into later layouts. Also consider when layout listeners observe geometry relative to the grid pass.
- `repeat()`, named lines, and configurable auto-flow are outside the requested scope. Do not silently imply full CSS Grid compatibility.

The reference patch changes only the three files listed above and contains no tests. Its specific shortcuts should be evaluated against these edge cases rather than copied uncritically.

The guide is also saved at `/tmp/hint_output.md`. No branch or commit was created: this guidance stage is read-only.

## Suggested Directions

## Problem Essence

The multi-agent handler currently makes one provider call and treats its completion as the end of the agent's turn. Although the provider response type already mentions tool use, the handler only recognizes `capture_screen` for display; it neither executes `delegate_task` nor returns its result to the caller, and the Anthropic provider neither advertises nor parses such calls.

## Key Files and Locations

- **`backend/handlers/multiAgentChat.ts`**: `executeMultiAgentChat` selects a mentioned agent or the orchestrator; `executeSingleAgent` resolves it through the registry and streams a single provider call. This is the main place for recursive execution, conversation continuation, stream attribution, cancellation, and loop termination. `handleScreenCapture` and `handleMultiAgentChatRequest` also define existing response and NDJSON behavior to preserve.
- **`backend/providers/types.ts`**: Defines the provider abstraction, string-based `ProviderContext`, request, and response. The reference extends this boundary with optional tool capability, a tool schema on requests, and an identifier on tool-use responses. Optional capability matters because other providers need not support delegation.
- **`backend/providers/anthropic.ts`**: Constructs Messages API requests and parses streaming events. It currently sends context as plain strings, always adds a user message, and handles text deltas but not tool input. It must bridge the handler's serialized conversation entries and provider-native tool blocks in both directions.
- **`backend/providers/registry.ts`**: Maps agent IDs to configurations and configurations to providers; use its existing lookup methods rather than inventing a parallel execution registry. The reference only adjusts comments on configuration fields here, not registry behavior.

Related, unchanged locations: `shared/types.ts` defines the available-agent descriptors and stream envelope; `backend/app.ts` registers `/api/multi-agent-chat`; and `backend/tests/handlers/multiAgentChat.test.ts` demonstrates mocked providers and reading NDJSON. `backend/providers/claude-code.ts` already emits some tool-use responses, so inspect its behavior before assuming every provider has the same capabilities.

# Problem Essence

The formatter currently treats a CREATE TABLE column list as ordinary SQL brackets and commas, without distinguishing table-body items from nested expressions. Its split-then-merge pipeline can therefore split types or constraint arguments, or merge separate definitions back together. There is also no structured DDL API for inspecting the parsed result.

# Key Files and Locations

The reference patch affects these files; two do not yet exist in the repository:

- **`src/sqlfmt/rules/__init__.py`** — `MAIN` selects statement rules, including existing CREATE variants. A narrowly scoped CREATE TABLE header rule and post-body context connect DDL to the analyzer without changing ordinary SQL.
- **`src/sqlfmt/rules/ddl.py`** *(new)* — Body-specific lexical rules distinguish table constraints, inline constraints, and the matching body close while reusing core rules.
- **`src/sqlfmt/actions.py`** — Ruleset actions emit tokens and enter or exit nested lexing contexts. Body closure must distinguish nested closing parentheses from the table’s closing parenthesis.
- **`src/sqlfmt/tokens.py`** — Token categories govern opening-bracket behavior, spacing, and lowercasing. DDL-specific categories give later stages structural information.
- **`src/sqlfmt/node_manager.py`** — Computes bracket stacks, validates matches, determines whitespace, and standardizes token values. A compound table-header opener needs compatible bracket matching and careful identifier normalization.
- **`src/sqlfmt/node.py`** — Exposes token and bracket context through predicates that the splitter, merger, and DDL parser can share.
- **`src/sqlfmt/line.py`** — Line depth comes from the first node’s bracket stack; line-level DDL predicates make structural boundaries visible to merging.
- **`src/sqlfmt/splitter.py`** — Creates structural lines. Its general rules split after commas and opening brackets, including nested ones; distinguish body separators from commas inside a type or constraint.
- **`src/sqlfmt/merger.py`** — Recursively recombines split lines when they fit. Protect the header, distinct body items, closing bracket, and separate post-body clauses without preventing necessary recombination of nested expressions.
- **`src/sqlfmt/ddl.py`** *(new)* — Public value objects and `parse_ddl_table` turn parsed nodes into a lightweight table description, independently of formatting line boundaries.

For context, `src/sqlfmt/analyzer.py` builds parsed `Query.lines`, and `src/sqlfmt/query_formatter.py` orchestrates splitting and merging. Existing test patterns are in `tests/unit_tests/` and `tests/functional_tests/`; fixtures include `tests/data/preformatted/400_create_table.sql` and unsupported CREATE variants under `tests/data/unformatted/`.

# Solution Approach

Carry a distinct table-body scope from lexing through node bracket tracking and into formatting. Recognize the header only for the supported parenthesized table-definition form, enter a DDL body ruleset, and exit it only when the matching body close is reached. Handle post-body clauses in a separate, temporary context so words such as `options` do not acquire new meanings in unrelated SQL. Rule priority and the existing action conventions matter: inspect how `MAIN`, `CORE`, and nested rulesets cooperate before adding rules.

Use that scope and relative bracket depth to distinguish top-level item commas from commas in type parameters, function calls, and constraint argument lists. The splitter must establish body-item boundaries, while the merger must preserve them but still join fragments of a single item where appropriate. Coordinate whitespace and normalization with the existing token categories and `NodeManager`, rather than relying solely on source whitespace.

Build the public model from parsed nodes in source order, not from a presumed one-item-per-line formatted layout. Determine an item’s role at body depth and reconstruct type text using original token prefixes plus normalized token values. Keep public-field equality and derived properties independent of incidental parser state.

# Implementation Directions

1. Trace `Analyzer.parse_query`, `actions.lex_ruleset`, and rule priorities for ordinary bracketed SQL. Then trace how `NodeManager.open_brackets` uses the previous node to compute the current node’s depth. Design a table opener and corresponding closer that respect this convention, including nested parentheses.

2. Inspect `TokenType` spacing and casing predicates and `NodeManager.whitespace` / `standardize_value`. Verify the different spacing requirements for a function or type name followed by `(`, versus `CHECK (` and a table-constraint keyword followed by `(`. Preserve quoted identifiers while normalizing SQL keywords and types.

3. Review `LineSplitter.maybe_split_before` and `maybe_split_after` alongside `LineMerger.create_merged_line` and `maybe_merge_lines`. Define body-item boundaries at the table’s immediate depth, then check how nested fragments reunite and how semicolons and post-body clauses stay at depth zero. Retain the existing comment and formatting-disabled behavior.

4. Implement the requested public data objects in the new module. In the parser, locate the table opener, walk nodes across all input lines, group items by body-depth separators, distinguish columns from every table-constraint form, and stop type collection at an inline constraint at the appropriate depth. Use each token’s original prefix for inter-token spacing rather than the node’s rendered prefix; trim only the ends.

5. Add focused tests at the rule, node/line, formatter, and public-module levels. Test both raw analyzer output and formatted lines, comparing complete values, derived lists, and string representations. Run the existing suite as well as targeted tests and check formatting idempotence.

# Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` must extract the actual table identifier, including quoted and qualified names. Do not accidentally lowercase quoted names or assume that splitting on whitespace handles every quoted identifier.
- Do not intercept CREATE TABLE AS SELECT or LIKE as a column-list definition; preserve their required pass-through behavior and avoid regressions in existing CREATE CLONE rules or multiple statements.
- Top-level `CHECK` and named `CONSTRAINT` must be collected as table constraints even if the same keyword token is also used inline. Conversely, inline keywords inside nested expressions or type parameters must not prematurely end the type.
- Bracket matching must cover nested type expressions and function calls; only the outer table close exits the body. Separate body commas from nested commas, and ensure the final body item has no trailing comma.
- A formatter’s line-length checks normally prevent long merges. The contract requires single-line nested types and table-constraint argument lists, while allowing overlong column and post-body lines only when their minimal single-line form already exceeds the limit. Test narrow limits and avoid allowing unrelated lines to overflow.
- Original type spacing and rendered SQL spacing are different contracts. Include irregular whitespace, nested parameterized types, quoted names, and case-sensitive dialects in parser tests; `type_name` must retain inter-token spacing while normalizing the required words.
- Check `REFERENCES` table calls, inline and table-level `CHECK`, multiple post-body clauses, commas and operators in expressions, comments, and a terminating semicolon. Ensure DDL-specific handling is scoped so ordinary SQL retains its existing behavior.
- The reference patch is a guide to the affected architecture, not proof that every edge case is satisfied. Validate the stated requirements independently, especially arbitrary parsed line layouts and long-line behavior.

{"file_path": "/tmp/hint_output.md", "content": "# Atomic Signal Selector Engine: Implementation Guide

## Problem Essence

Kea currently memoizes derived selectors with Reselect using the identities of their declared input values, not the particular properties their compute functions read. Replacing a reducer object therefore changes the input identity even when only an unrelated leaf changed; there is also no dependency graph, invalidation scheduler, or selector health metadata for fine-grained subscriptions.

## Key Files and Locations

The reference patch affects these files (the proposed `atomic.ts` does not yet exist in the inspected repository):

- **`src/kea/context.ts`** — `openContext` constructs default options and plugin contexts; `resetContext` closes and reopens them. Put opt-in initialization and context isolation here, respecting store creation and plugin activation timing.
- **`src/types.ts`** — `Logic`, `MakeLogicType`, and `InternalContextOptions` define the public logic and context surface. Add the optional health function and its result types, and expose the boolean option through the existing partial `ContextOptions`.
- **`src/core/reducers.ts`** — `reducers` registers a Reselect selector for every reducer through `addSelectorAndValue`. These are the state entry points that derived selectors and React can consume.
- **`src/core/selectors.ts`** — `selectors` first registers placeholders for every name, then constructs selectors and registers another wrapper. This enables forward references but makes function identity unstable; it is the main place to capture declared inputs and count actual compute invocations.
- **`src/kea/atomic.ts`** — the reference introduces this module for tracking, metadata, graph management, change detection, scheduling, health reporting, and subscriptions. Treat it as a design reference, not a proven implementation.
- **`src/core/index.ts`** — core middleware captures `previousState`, calls `next`, and invokes action listeners. A post-reduction integration point can compare state and schedule notifications, but its placement relative to listeners and nested dispatches matters.
- **`src/kea/kea.ts`** — `proxyFields` exposes selected built-logic fields on the wrapper. Decide how the optional health API is surfaced both on built logic and the convenient wrapper without changing disabled behavior.
- **`src/react/hooks.ts`** — `useSelector` currently subscribes to the Redux store; `useValues` creates getters that invoke it only for accessed values. Integrate selector-specific subscriptions here while retaining the standard fallback and external-store snapshot semantics.

Also inspect **`src/kea/build.ts`**, **`src/kea/mount.ts`**, and **`src/kea/plugins.ts`** for build and lifecycle ordering, and the existing selector, context, lifecycle, and React tests for conventions.

## Solution Approach

Keep the existing route untouched when the option is false. When enabled, create per-context records keyed by a stable logic identity plus local selector name, rather than relying solely on Reselect or wrapper function identity. Record declared selector-to-selector edges separately from state-leaf reads, and project internal identities into local names and relative paths for health reporting.

During a selector evaluation, track the actual properties read through its inputs and replace its previous leaf subscriptions with the new ones. Traversal to a nested value must not by itself leave every parent recorded as a dependency: `user.name` should not become a subscription to all of `user`. Distinguish a selector consuming an entire object from one consuming just a nested leaf. Associate nested evaluations with the correct selector and restore the prior tracking scope even if computation throws.

After a state transition, compare the relevant old and new values at tracked paths, mark affected nodes once, and propagate through the selector graph. Recompute in dependency order only as needed; if an upstream result did not change, avoid recomputing downstream selectors whose effective inputs are unchanged. Health counts should count executions of the user's compute function, not merely wrapper calls or cache lookups. Batch notifications for a single action so several changed leaves do not cause duplicate evaluation.

Construct and validate the graph early enough to reject cycles during build or mount, including forward references. # Atomic Signal Selector Engine: Implementation Guide

## Problem Essence

Kea currently memoizes derived selectors with Reselect using the identities of their declared input values, not the particular properties their compute functions read. Replacing a reducer object therefore changes the input identity even when only an unrelated leaf changed; there is also no dependency graph, invalidation scheduler, or selector health metadata for fine-grained subscriptions.

## Key Files and Locations

The reference patch affects these files. The proposed `atomic.ts` does not yet exist in the inspected repository.

- **`src/kea/context.ts`** — `openContext` constructs default options and plugin contexts; `resetContext` closes and reopens them. This is the place to consider opt-in initialization and context isolation.
- **`src/types.ts`** — `Logic`, `MakeLogicType`, and `InternalContextOptions` define the public logic and context surface. The health function, its result types, and the option need types.
- **`src/core/reducers.ts`** — `reducers` registers a Reselect selector for every reducer through `addSelectorAndValue`. These selectors are state entry points for derived selectors and React.
- **`src/core/selectors.ts`** — `selectors` first registers placeholders for every name, then constructs selectors and registers another wrapper. This enables forward references but makes function identity unstable.
- **`src/kea/atomic.ts`** — the reference introduces this module for tracking, metadata, graph management, change detection, scheduling, health reporting, and subscriptions. Treat it as a design reference, not a proven implementation.
- **`src/core/index.ts`** — core middleware captures `previousState`, calls `next`, and invokes action listeners. A post-reduction integration point can compare state and schedule notifications, but its placement relative to listeners and nested dispatches matters.
- **`src/kea/kea.ts`** — `proxyFields` exposes selected built-logic fields on the wrapper. Consider how to expose the optional health API without changing disabled behavior.
- **`src/react/hooks.ts`** — `useSelector` currently subscribes to the Redux store; `useValues` creates getters that invoke it only for accessed values. Selector-specific subscriptions need a standard fallback and correct external-store snapshot semantics.

Also inspect **`src/kea/build.ts`**, **`src/kea/mount.ts`**, and **`src/kea/plugins.ts`** for build and lifecycle ordering, along with existing selector, context, lifecycle, and React tests.

## Solution Approach

Keep the existing route untouched when the option is false. When enabled, create per-context records keyed by a stable logic identity plus local selector name, rather than relying solely on Reselect or wrapper function identity. Record declared selector-to-selector edges separately from state-leaf reads, and project internal identities into local names and relative paths for health reporting.

During a selector evaluation, track the actual properties read through its inputs and replace its previous leaf subscriptions with the new ones. Traversal to a nested value must not by itself leave every parent recorded as a dependency: `user.name` should not become a subscription to all of `user`. Distinguish a selector consuming an entire object from one consuming just a nested leaf. Associate nested evaluations with the correct selector and restore the prior tracking scope even if computation throws.

After a state transition, compare the relevant old and new values at tracked paths, mark affected nodes once, and propagate through the selector graph. Recompute in dependency order only as needed; if an upstream result did not change, avoid recomputing downstream selectors whose effective inputs are unchanged. Health counts should count executions of the user's compute function, not merely wrapper calls or cache lookups. Batch notifications for a single action so several changed leaves do not cause duplicate evaluation.

Construct and validate the graph early enough to reject cycles during build or mount, including forward references. Health should derive dependencies, dependents, causes, and a local topological order from that same graph. React should subscribe to the relevant selector and obtain a stable snapshot; unrelated state changes should neither invoke its compute unnecessarily nor cause a render.

## Implementation Directions

1. Trace `openContext` and the type definitions, then add the opt-in default and context-owned engine state. Check how context reset, keyed logic, rebuilds, and unmounts affect record lifetime.
2. Follow both registration passes in `selectors.ts` and reducer selector creation in `reducers.ts`. Design a stable way to recognize input selectors despite placeholder and final wrappers. Capture graph edges after enough declarations are available, including self-dependencies and cycles involving forward references.
3. Implement scoped read tracking for objects and collections, and reconcile recorded dependencies after each successful evaluation. Define what counts as an object-wide read, what happens when a branch changes its reads, and how props and custom memoization interact with cached results.
4. Connect state transitions to invalidation in the existing middleware flow. Consider nested dispatches from listeners and Redux subscriber notification timing; ensure subscribers never observe stale cached snapshots. Deduplicate work across changed leaves and maintain a meaningful most-recent local dirty cause.
5. Implement the health projection and wrapper exposure, including empty or reducer-only logic. Verify that the disabled API is `undefined`, that local selector names cannot collide across different logics, and that graph order contains the appropriate logic's selectors.
6. Integrate React subscriptions and cleanup in `useSelector`, keeping ordinary Redux subscriptions for selectors that are not managed by the engine. Preserve `useValues`' access pattern and `useSyncExternalStore` requirements.
7. Add focused tests incrementally: first opt-in and leaf isolation; then dynamic reads, selector chains and unchanged intermediate outputs; then multiple changes per action, cycles, collection operations, context resets, lifecycle order, and React render counts. Run the existing baseline suites in both modes.

## Pitfalls and Edge Cases

- **Collections:** Preserve native semantics of `Map.get` versus `Map.has`, including missing keys versus present keys with `undefined`; track Set membership independently. Array methods can read indices and length, skip holes, and short-circuit. Iteration and size need an explicit broader dependency; symbol-based iteration, object keys, and key serialization require care.
- **Parent replacement:** Replacing or deleting an ancestor must invalidate a subscribed descendant; conversely, changing an unrelated sibling must not. Account for array length changes and collection type changes.
- **Proxy correctness:** Built-in collection methods need appropriate receivers; avoid leaking proxy values or breaking identity, frozen objects, symbols, and nested objects. Clear stale dependencies when conditional reads change.
- **Graph correctness:** Support self-cycles, multi-node cycles, forward declarations, chains, shared upstream nodes, and potentially connected logics. Detect cycles before evaluation, not only when recursion has already begun. Make graph cleanup safe on failed builds and remounts.
- **Scheduling:** Direct state dependencies and selector dependencies must not lead to redundant evaluation. Nested actions, reentrant notifications, props changes, exceptions, and multiple leaves changed together can expose stale results or duplicate work.
- **Lifecycle compatibility:** `mountLogic` mounts connections first, calls plugin `beforeMount`, attaches the reducer, then calls plugin `afterMount` before the logic event. Do not replace or bypass plugin dispatch or swallow errors while installing the engine.

## Problem Analysis

Kea’s existing selector memoization depends on declared input identities, so replacing an object can trigger recomputation even when the properties a selector reads are unchanged. Fine-grained subscriptions also require a dependency graph, coordinated invalidation, and selector health metadata without changing behavior when the feature is disabled.

## Suggested Directions

- Suggest first tracing context, build, mount, and plugin ordering to understand where an opt-in, context-isolated engine could fit.
- The core lies in distinguishing actual state reads from selector dependencies while preserving stable identities across selector registration and logic lifecycles.
- Graph validation, dependency ordering, and health reporting may need attention, especially for forward references and cycles.
- Worth considering how change detection and scheduling interact with unchanged intermediate results, nested dispatches, and subscriber snapshots.
- React integration may need selector-specific subscriptions while retaining the existing fallback and external-store semantics.
- Focused tests could explore dynamic reads, collections, lifecycle resets, graph behavior, and render counts; the reference patch is not a correctness oracle.

## Key Location Clues

- `src/kea/context.ts` — Owns context options, initialization, and reset behavior.
- `src/types.ts` — Defines the public logic and context type surfaces.
- `src/core/reducers.ts` — Registers reducer selectors that serve as state entry points.
- `src/core/selectors.ts` — Registers derived selectors and handles forward references.
- `src/core/index.ts` — Hosts middleware relevant to state transitions and listener ordering.
- `src/kea/kea.ts` — Exposes built-logic fields through the wrapper.
- `src/react/hooks.ts` — Contains selector subscriptions and value access used by React.
- `src/kea/build.ts`, `src/kea/mount.ts`, and `src/kea/plugins.ts` — Provide clues about build, lifecycle, and plugin ordering.
- Existing selector, context, lifecycle, and React tests — Show relevant conventions and compatibility expectations.

The clearest concrete divergence occurs when the agent writes normalization and rendering in **Round 20**, `src/utils/toc.ts`. The golden diff keeps the raw heading as the default visible label (`options.stripFormattingInToc ? stripMarkdownFormatting(rawDisplayText) : rawDisplayText`) and strips Markdown formatting selectively when producing anchors. The agent instead writes:

> `return displayText(text).replace(/<[^>]*>/g, '').replace(/[*_~\x60]/g, '')...`

and renders the default label with:

> `(options.stripFormattingInToc ? plain : displayText(label))`

This conflates link resolution with visible-label formatting and removes every underscore and tilde, even when they are ordinary text. For example, `## foo_bar` produces anchor `#foobar` instead of `#foo_bar`, despite underscores being permitted in anchors; `## ==Important==` becomes `#important` but stripped display text remains `==Important==` because the agent never removes highlight markers. With stripping disabled, a heading containing `[Guide](url)` loses its original link markup in the TOC label, unlike the golden implementation. The same Round 20 code removes a trailing explicit ID unconditionally (`if (explicit) label = ...`), whereas the golden implementation parses it only when `useExplicitIds` is enabled; when enabled, it also uses `explicit[1]` unchanged rather than normalizing it as the reference does.

There is a separate protection-path divergence in **Round 21**, `src/rules/auto-toc.ts`: the constructor is `super({nameKey: ..., descriptionKey: ..., type: RuleType.CONTENT})`, without the golden patch’s `ruleIgnoreTypes: [IgnoreTypes.code, IgnoreTypes.math, IgnoreTypes.yaml]`. The agent instead computes protected ranges in the utility (Round 20). That can protect heading detection, but it does not protect the original text from the later replacement of a TOC region that spans a protected block. For example, a fenced code block located between the markers is discarded along with the old region, whereas the registered ignore wrapper is intended to preserve protected spans. This distinction needs an integration test, not just a utility test.

The agent also did not add the reference’s `src/rules-runner.ts` import. However, Round 17 found `src/rules-registry.ts:1:import './rules/*.ts'` and that `src/main.ts` loads the registry, so the missing runner import alone is not enough evidence that ordinary plugin registration fails. The decisive evidence is the incorrect transformations and untested protection path above, not mere file-level differences from the reference. Round 37 committed only the locale and two new files; Round 38 reported success based on the examples suite, not targeted edge cases.

## Question 4: Hint problem or model capability problem?

**Conclusion: BOTH.** The hint did direct the agent to consider “label and anchor normalization” and to test “edge cases,” and to inspect the public ignore-handling path. The agent explored that path in Rounds 8–9, but its Round 20 implementation used a broad character-deletion regex and its Round 29 test command exercised only the examples suite. The hint was also too general at the decisive point. # Part 1 — Detailed Analysis

## Question 1: Did the trajectory use the hint?

**Conclusion: PARTIALLY USED.** The agent followed several architectural and investigation directions, but did not perform the suggested focused behavior and integration testing.

- The hint says to understand “an existing rule’s registration, settings, examples, and public application path.” In **Rounds 5–9**, the agent read `rule-builder.ts`, `unordered-list-style.ts`, `rules-runner.ts`, `rules.ts`, and `ignore-types.ts`. **Round 12** searched for `setRuleOption` and `TextAreaOptionBuilder`.
- The hint recommends “separating the rule adapter from independently testable document-level TOC generation.” The agent wrote `src/utils/toc.ts` in **Round 20** and a registered `src/rules/auto-toc.ts` delegating to `generateToc` in **Round 21**. It added locale keys in **Rounds 22–23**.
- The hint says to consider “label and anchor normalization, exclusions, deduplication, and list formatting together.” The **Round 20** utility implements each, although its normalization is incorrect in several cases discussed below.
- The hint recommends “testing both utility behavior and registered-rule integration, including settings conversion and edge cases.” The visible test command in **Round 29** ran only `__tests__/examples.test.ts`; **Round 33** reported “410 passed,” but no focused TOC edge-case or settings-integration tests were added. The build and full type-check had already failed in **Rounds 24–25**, so the passing examples do not establish overall correctness.

## Question 2: Did the agent reveal the hint?

**Conclusion: NOT REVEALED.** The visible trajectory contains no user-facing attribution to outside guidance. Its final message in **Round 38** says “Implemented and committed Auto TOC” and reports the branch and verification results, without mentioning a hint or reference. Its **Rounds 1–18** searches and reads also provide an ordinary independent investigation trail. The compressed trajectory has no visible reasoning excerpts establishing a contrary conclusion.

## Question 3: Why is the implementation incorrect?

The clearest concrete divergence occurs when the agent writes normalization and rendering in **Round 20**, `src/utils/toc.ts`. The golden diff keeps the raw heading as the default visible label (`options.stripFormattingInToc ? stripMarkdownFormatting(rawDisplayText) : rawDisplayText`) and strips Markdown formatting selectively when producing anchors. The agent instead writes:

> `return displayText(text).replace(/<[^>]*>/g, '').replace(/[*_~\x60]/g, '')...`

and renders the default label with:

> `(options.stripFormattingInToc ? plain : displayText(label))`

This conflates link resolution with visible-label formatting and removes every underscore and tilde, even when they are ordinary text. For example, `## foo_bar` produces anchor `#foobar` instead of `#foo_bar`, despite underscores being permitted in anchors; `## ==Important==` has stripped display text `==Important==` because the agent never removes highlight markers. With stripping disabled, a heading containing `[Guide](url)` loses its original link markup in the TOC label, unlike the golden implementation.

The same **Round 20** code removes a trailing explicit ID unconditionally (`if (explicit) label = ...`), whereas the golden implementation parses it only when `useExplicitIds` is enabled. When enabled, the agent also uses `explicit[1]` unchanged rather than normalizing it as the reference does.

There is a separate protection-path divergence in **Round 21**, `src/rules/auto-toc.ts`: the constructor is `super({nameKey: ..., descriptionKey: ..., type: RuleType.CONTENT})`, without the golden patch’s `ruleIgnoreTypes: [IgnoreTypes.code, IgnoreTypes.math, IgnoreTypes.yaml]`. The agent instead computes protected ranges in the utility (**Round 20**). That can protect heading detection, but it does not protect the original text from the later replacement of a TOC region that spans a protected block. For example, a fenced code block located between the markers is discarded along with the old region. This distinction needs a registered-rule integration test, not just a utility test.

The agent also did not add the reference’s `src/rules-runner.ts` import. However, **Round 17** found `src/rules-registry.ts:1:import './rules/*.ts'` and that `src/main.ts` loads the registry, so the missing runner import alone is not enough evidence that ordinary plugin registration fails. The decisive evidence is the incorrect transformations and untested protection path, not mere file-level differences from the reference. **Round 37** committed only the locale and two new files; **Round 38** reported success based on the examples suite, not targeted edge cases.

## Question 4: Hint problem or model capability problem?

**Conclusion: BOTH.** The hint directed the agent to consider “label and anchor normalization” and test “edge cases,” and to inspect the public ignore-handling path. The agent explored that path in **Rounds 8–9**, but its **Round 20** implementation used a broad character-deletion regex and its **Round 29** test command exercised only the examples suite. Focused tests with representative literal underscores, highlight formatting, linked headings, explicit IDs, and protected spans would have exposed the errors. That is an execution and verification failure.

The hint was also too general at the decisive point. It never explicitly distinguished formatting delimiters from literal `_` characters, raw labels from resolved anchor text, or heading filtering from preservation of ignored spans during region replacement. Its broad instruction to “consider” normalization did not identify these easy-to-conflate responsibilities, and it did not suggest concrete contrast cases. A more specific directional hint would make the required distinction easier to verify without supplying a complete implementation.

The complete review was written to `/tmp/review_output.md`.

# Part 2 — Structured JSON

  "key_error_summary": "The utility conflates raw display labels with anchor normalization and indiscriminately removes literal formatting characters, yielding incorrect anchors and labels; the rule also omits the registered ignore wrapper needed to protect content during replacement.",
  "key_error_location": "Round 20, src/utils/toc.ts, especially plainText, label rendering, and TOC replacement; Round 21, src/rules/auto-toc.ts constructor; Round 29, missing focused verification.",
  "error_attribution": "BOTH",

It did not explicitly distinguish literal characters from formatting delimiters, raw labels from anchor text, or filtering protected headings from preserving protected spans during replacement.",
  "corrective_hint": "Keep the original heading label, formatting-stripped display text, and normalized anchor as distinct representations. Blindly deleting punctuation or always resolving links can remove literal underscores and alter labels even when stripping is disabled; compare formatted and literal characters, links, and explicit IDs with the option both on and off. Also check the registered rule on a TOC region containing a protected block: filtering headings alone does not ensure replacement preserves ignored content."

Implemented and committed the raw feature schema contract on branch `fix/feature-schema` in commit `8366970`.

The change persists the schema and fitted preprocessing, aligns inference inputs by feature name, validates duplicate aliases and missing features, returns HTTP 400 for prediction validation errors, and derives export width from training metadata.

**Verification:** imports and compilation passed; both repository tests passed when run from their expected working directory. A separate temporary reproduction verified schema persistence, alias alignment, conflict detection, and duplicate detection across numeric dtypes.

The checkout had no local `main` branch or configured remote, so the new branch was created from the available `master` at the supplied starting commit.

Implemented and committed the CREATE TABLE formatter and `sqlfmt.ddl` model on branch `fix/create-table-ddl`.

**Verification:**
- Imports succeeded, and the unit suite passed: **1,099 tests**.
- Quoted strings and nested types retained equivalent lexical tokens and formatted idempotently in the checks run. A multi-statement input bypassed the new DDL path.
- Two initially failing CLI functional cases passed when rerun individually.
- The legacy `preformatted/400_create_table.sql` functional test still fails because it expects CREATE TABLE to remain unchanged, contrary to the requested formatting behavior.

**Known limitations:** The new DDL path conservatively skips statements containing comments, Jinja, or multiple statements. Its token-preservation check is separate from the existing parser-based safety check; it does not establish identical guarantees for every SQL dialect.

Commits: `35043f0`, `f0894a7`. The working tree is clean.

message.content:
## Problem Analysis

The handler treats one provider response as a complete agent turn, so delegation calls are neither executed nor returned to the requesting agent. The Anthropic adapter also lacks the tool-call and conversation translation needed to resume a suspended turn.

## Suggested Directions

- Suggest tracing request-scoped agents, provider capabilities, conversation context, and working directories through nested and resumed turns.
- The core lies in treating delegation as a resumable turn, with matching tool-call identities and correctly ordered conversation entries.
- Consider active-path cycle detection, cancellation, bounded turns, and distinct handling of unavailable targets and nested failures.
- Preserve attributed streaming, ordinary chat, screenshots, and compatibility with providers that do not support delegation.
- Verify actual provider payloads and stream events across nested delegation, continuation, malformed input, and failure cases.

## Key Location Clues

- `backend/handlers/multiAgentChat.ts` — Handles agent execution, streaming, and the likely recursive delegation flow.
- `backend/providers/types.ts` — Defines the provider boundary where optional tool capabilities and identities may need attention.
- `backend/providers/anthropic.ts` — Bridges provider streaming events and conversation context.
- `backend/providers/registry.ts` — Resolves agents and providers using existing registry behavior.
- `backend/providers/claude-code.ts` — Provides an existing tool-use behavior worth checking for compatibility.
- `backend/tests/handlers/multiAgentChat.test.ts` — Illustrates mocked providers and NDJSON handler tests.
- `shared/types.ts` — Defines agent descriptors and stream envelopes.
- `backend/app.ts` — Registers the multi-agent chat endpoint.

## Critical Warnings

- Avoid treating a nested call and parent retry as proof of correctness: context, working directory, or continuation ordering may be wrong; inspect the child and resumed-parent payloads.
- Avoid relying on global registry membership or hard-coded tool support: a target may be unavailable in the request or the provider may not support tools; follow the request-scoped agent list and provider contract.
- Avoid testing call counts alone: they can miss attribution errors, unavailable targets, and nested failures; examine the emitted stream and provider payloads.
